It also does not support the citation record's own wording that Withania is 'classed among the principal restoratives' in a rasayana chapter; I grepped all 24 ashwagandha occurrences in the OCR and in the actual rasayana material (Chikitsasthana I, lines 69230, 73356, 76346, 76706, 99339 etc.) Ashwagandha appears only as the modern SUBSTITUTE for the unidentifiable drug Meda, e.g. line 69230 "(Meda)  which  being  unobtainable,  Agwagandha  or  Physalis".
concerns: Two characters were silently normalized from OCR noise: the source prints "Rishabhi  («)" and "Sthira  {z)" where the excerpt gives "(u)" and "(z)". The footnote list itself confirms u and z are the right letters, so this is defensible cleanup rather than invention, but it is a deviation from strict verbatim and should be disclosed if the excerpt is stored as a quotation.

The transcription 'Afwagandha' is itself an OCR rendering of the book's diacritical spelling; a reader searching for 'Ashwagandha' in this file finds nothing. Anyone re-checking must search 'wagandha'.

The locator field quotes the chapter as "'These are the fifty Astringents par excellence'". The book actually reads "The fifty Astringents par excellence that have been spoken of shall now be indicated." The locator is paraphrasing, which is how a locator that does not resolve gets past a checker. It does resolve here, but the quoted form is not the book's.
The stored URL is dead (404) and its metadata endpoint is empty. The citation as stored points at nothing; only the substituted item ID reaches the text.

The row's stored energetics (Warm; Bitter/Astringent/Sweet; Dry) are nighantu-tradition values. The cited work is silent on all three. After this verification the row still has no pre-1900 support for temperature, taste or moisture.

results.whatIFound: I downloaded Project Gutenberg ebook 49513 (pg49513.txt, 1,531,341 bytes; Title: The Complete Herbal, Author: Nicholas Culpeper) and read the HYSSOP entry at lines 6935-6968. Both quoted sentences are present character for character within the '_Government and virtues._]' paragraph: "It helps to expectorate tough phlegm, and is effectual in all cold griefs or diseases of the chests or lungs, being taken either in syrup or licking medicine." and "Dioscorides saith, that Hyssop boiled with rue and honey, and drank, helps those that are troubled with coughs, shortness of breath, wheezing and rheumatic distillation upon the lungs". I also searched the whole file for any degree grading of Hyssop: it is absent from every one of Culpeper's herb degree lists (lines 18584-18628, 'Herbs temperate in respect of heat' / 'hot in the first / second / third / fourth degree' / 'dry in the first / second degree'). Hyssop DOES appear in the appended Dispensatory's organ lists — 'Heat the breast' (line 18675) and 'Heat the liver' (line 18691).
results.supportsTheClaim: It supports the indication set precisely — expectoration of tough phlegm, cough, wheezing, shortness of breath, rheumatic distillation on the lungs, and the qualifier 'all cold griefs or diseases of the chests or lungs'. It does NOT state a temperature. 'Effectual in all cold griefs of the lungs' says what the herb is used AGAINST, not what the herb IS; Culpeper grades scores of herbs by explicit degree and gives Hyssop none, which I verified by exhaustive search rather than by inference. It supports no taste at all, and specifically not Astringent.
concerns: ORDER INVERSION. The excerpt joins the two sentences with '[...]' in the order expectorate-first, Dioscorides-second. In the source the Dioscorides sentence comes near the START of the paragraph and the expectorate sentence near the END. The bracketed ellipsis implies forward continuation and misrepresents the passage's shape. Both sentences are genuine; the sequencing is not.

The strongest warmth evidence in Culpeper for Hyssop is NOT the cited passage but the appended Dispensatory's organ lists, where Hyssop appears under 'Heat the breast' and 'Heat the liver'. That is still not a degree grading, but it is closer to a thermal statement than anything in the quoted material, and it is uncited.
The row's Astringent taste has no support in either named work. I found no taste statement for Hyssop anywhere in the Culpeper file.
The citation's own stored URL points at botanical.com, i.e. the Grieve half, not at any Culpeper edition. A reader following the stored link never reaches the text that is actually doing the work.
The entry opens with 'The herb is Jupiter's, and the sign Cancer' — correctly excluded by the finder, and I confirm the clinical material quoted is separable from it.

The stored URL does not reach the entry. anethum.html under /kings/ is a confirmed 404; the live slug is anethum_fructus.html. A checker guessing the obvious filename gets nothing and may wrongly conclude the entry does not exist.

I separately downloaded 本草綱目 (四庫全書本) 卷14 (184,742 bytes): the 芍藥 entry is anchored at offset 15372 with the note 本經中品, and the 氣味 anchor at offset ~16060 prints 氣味苦平無毒, with the following note 别錄曰酸微寒有小毒普曰神農苦桐君甘無毒岐伯鹹雷公酸李當之小寒元素曰性寒味酸…, and the 主治 line 主治邪氣腹痛除血痺破堅積寒熱疝瘕止痛利小便益氣 attributed to 本經.
results.supportsTheClaim: It supports the indications only: 主邪氣腹痛 and 止痛 for cramping abdominal pain, 除血痹 for the blood-impediment/blood-nourishing framing, 破堅積、寒熱、疝瘕 and 利小便 for the rest. It DOES NOT support temperature=Cool. The source says 平, NEUTRAL, and Bencao Gangmu independently confirms 本經's reading as 苦平. It DOES NOT support taste=Sour; the source says 苦, BITTER. It does not distinguish white from red peony anywhere.
concerns: TEMPERATURE IS CONTRADICTED, NOT MERELY UNSUPPORTED. The row stores Cool; the named source says 平 (neutral). This is the same failure shape as the withdrawn Ginkgo citation. A source that states the opposite of the stored field is worse than a source that is silent, because the citation lends authority to a value the work refutes.

TASTE IS ALSO CONTRADICTED. The row stores Sour; 神農本草經 says 苦 (bitter). 'Sour' appears in this recension only inside the appended 吳普 attribution list, which I read at line 1584: 神農：苦；桐君：甘，無毒；岐伯：咸；李氏：小寒；雷公：酸 — five named authorities disagreeing, with sour being Lei Gong's minority reading and Shennong's own being bitter. Quoting the entry as support for Sour inverts what it says.
Cool and Sour ARE available pre-1900, but from a different source. BCGM 卷14 records 别錄曰酸微寒有小毒 and 元素曰性寒味酸. If the row wants Cool and Sour it must cite Mingyi Bielu via BCGM, not the Shennong classic.

SPECIES/PREPARATION GAP. The Shennong text has one undifferentiated 芍藥. Everything the row claims that is specific to the peeled, boiled WHITE root is outside this source. The Bai/Chi split is BCGM-era; I read it at offset 16725 of 卷14 (成無已曰白補而赤瀉白收而赤散) and at 17001 (時珍曰白芍藥益脾能於土中瀉木赤芍藥散邪能行血中之滯).
The excerpt stops mid-line at 益氣 without an ellipsis; the source continues （《藝文類聚》引云：一名白朮。《大觀本》作黑字）。 Truncation is normal, but the excerpt should be marked as ending early.

S. P.)." Under 'Action, Medical Uses, and Dosage.': "Geranium is a powerful astringent. Used in infusion with milk in the second stage of dysentery, diarrhoea, and cholera infantum. In bowel disorders it is the chronic or subacute states in which it is applicable, and especially where the discharges are abundant and debilitating. The relaxation of membranes following the inflammatory stage is an indication for its use." and, after the marked ellipsis, "From its freedom from any nauseous or unpleasant qualities, it is well adapted to infants and persons with fastidious stomachs." 'Specific Indications and Uses.—Relaxed mucous tissues, with profuse, debilitating discharges; chronic diarrhoea, with mucous discharges; chronic dysentery; diarrhoea, with constant desire to evacuate the bowels; passive hemorrhages.' is complete and exact. I then grepped the full stripped entry for refrigerant / cooling / cool / cold / febrifuge / warming: the ONLY hit is 'Cold weather does not kill it', in the Erodium cicutarium forage-plant paragraph.
results.supportsTheClaim: It supports TASTE strongly — 'taste strongly astringent' in the U.S.P. description and 'Geranium is a powerful astringent' in Felter & Lloyd's own first sentence. It supports the freedom-from-nauseous-qualities claim and the whole indication set: relaxed mucous tissues, profuse debilitating discharges, chronic diarrhoea and dysentery, passive haemorrhage. It DOES NOT support temperature in any degree. King's is Eclectic and assigns Geranium no thermal value; I verified this by exhaustive keyword search, not by impression. It also does not support the row's aerial-parts claim.
concerns: TEMPERATURE IS UNSUPPORTED AND THE ROW SUPPLIES ITS OWN REASONING. The row stores Cool and justifies it in-field with 'A tannin astringent is cooling and condensing'. That is the row inferring from chemistry, not the source speaking. Cited as if King's backed it, this is precisely the pattern where a real quote gets attached to a field it cannot underwrite.

BITTERNESS IS THE WRONG SPECIES. The row's 'mild bitterness' traces to King's phrase 'a disagreeable, bitterish, astringent taste', which I confirmed appears in the Related Species paragraph describing GERANIUM ROBERTIANUM (Herb Robert), not G. maculatum. G. maculatum's own taste statement is 'inodorous; taste strongly astringent' — no bitterness at all. A congener's taste has been imported into the species row.

PARAPHRASE DRIFT PRESENTED AS QUOTATION. The row says King's lists it as 'free of any nauseous or acrid quality'. King's wrote 'freedom from any nauseous or unpleasant qualities'. 'Unpleasant' became 'acrid', which is a different pharmacological claim, and the row attributes it to King's.

PART-USED MISMATCH. The row's part_used says leaf and aerial parts are 'also astringent and are used as a gentler, more sustainable tea'. King's 1898 states flatly 'The dried root is the official part' and the U.S.P. description is entirely of the rhizome. The aerial-parts claim has zero support in the cited work.
The stored url is the section root, not geranium.html. A checker following it does not land on the entry.

I also checked the moisture lists at lines 19075-19084: 'Moist in the first degree' names citrons, lemons, oranges; 'In the second' gourds, melons, peaches, prunes; 'Dry in the first degree' juniper berries; 'In the second' Nut Ben, capers, pears, fistick nuts, pine nuts, quinces, nutmegs, bay berries. I separately fetched botanical.com/botanical/mgmh/f/figcom12.html (HTTP 200) and confirmed Grieve's 'It is considered that the laxative property resides in the saccharine juice of the fresh fruit' and 'The milky juice of the stems and leaves is very acrid'.
results.supportsTheClaim: The temperature claim is genuinely and explicitly supported: Culpeper files Figs under '_Temperate in respect of heat._', which maps directly onto the stored Neutral. That is a rare case in this batch of a pre-1900 source stating the stored temperature outright. The laxative and demulcent action on dry bowel and throat is supported ('they loose the belly'; 'dry figs help coughs, cleanse the breast'), as is the acrid latex ('The milk that issues out from the leaves or branches where they are broken off, being dropped upon warts, takes them away'). Moisture is NOT supported, and the stored taste is NOT supported.
concerns: MOISTURE IS UNSUPPORTED, AND THE SILENCE IS DELIBERATE ON CULPEPER'S PART. He gives explicit moist and dry degree lists in the same section and omits Figs from all four. A reader seeing a Culpeper citation on the row could easily assume the moisture field came from the same list. It did not.

TASTE 'Sweet (ripe fruit)' is stated as a taste in neither named source. Grieve's 'saccharine juice' is a statement about sugar content, post-1900, and forbidden for energetics under the project's own rule. The nearest thing to a taste word in Culpeper's Fig material is 'of ill juice' about green figs.

GREEN vs DRIED IS NOT RESOLVED. Culpeper's own Fig commentary explicitly opposes green figs (ill juice) to dry figs (the therapeutic ones), and the College's fruit catalogue at line 19031 lists 'Green Figs' separately. The 'Temperate in respect of heat' entry says only 'Figs' and does not say which. The row's temperature therefore rests on an undifferentiated list item.

POINTER FAILURE. The citation names Culpeper, but the stored url is the bare botanical.com domain (Grieve's host) and the locator field is the title string repeated. Nothing in the stored record directs a reader to the degree list, which is the only element carrying the temperature. This is the shape where a locator goes unchecked because there is nothing concrete to check.

The Fig-Tree entry closes with 'The tree is under the dominion of Jupiter' plus lightning and mad-bull folklore. Correctly excluded, and I confirm the clinical material sits before it and is separable.

results.supportsTheClaim: The Shennong entry supports taste 甘 (sweet), temperature 平 (neutral), and the shen-calming indication — 安五臟 (settles the five zang), 利/和心志 (settles the heart-mind), 令人歡樂無憂 (makes one joyful and free of worry). concerns: THE CITATION RECORD IS INTERNALLY BROKEN AND THE BREAK IS THE DANGEROUS KIND. Title names the Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing; author field reads 'King's American Dispensatory'; url points at henriettes-herb.com/eclectic/kings/. I verified King's has no Albizia entry under any of four plausible slugs — all 404. A reader trusting the author and url fields is sent to a work that does not contain this plant at all. This is the one-citation-naming-several-works shape from the withdrawal history.

EXACT-MATCH WARNING HANDLED, AND I AM RESTATING IT. The source reads 味甘，平 and the row stores taste=Sweet, temperature=Neutral — a precise two-field mirror, the Lion's Mane pattern. I chased it independently from raw wikitext I fetched myself and cross-checked against BCGM 卷35下, and it is genuine, not back-fabricated. But because the mirror is exact, this row should not be treated as independently corroborated by a second reader who used the same excerpt.

The BCGM secondary block in the excerpt carries commas and full stops that are NOT in the source. The Siku wikitext of 卷35下 is unpunctuated. The Shennong block's punctuation, by contrast, IS in that recension. If the BCGM material is ever stored as a quotation, the added punctuation must be disclosed as editorial.

The corrupt 獻 was correctly left in place and flagged rather than silently emended — good practice, but it means the stored excerpt contains a character the compilers know is wrong. Store the emendation note with it or a later reader will 'fix' it invisibly.

PART-USED MISMATCH. The row distinguishes bark (He Huan Pi) from flower (He Huan Hua) and assigns blood-invigoration to the bark. Neither the Shennong entry nor BCGM's 木皮 section describes a separate flower drug; BCGM's only flower mention is the 夜合花枝 decoction in a 附方 for infant lockjaw.

WORLDVIEW MATERIAL CORRECTLY EXCLUDED. Both sources continue 久服輕身明目 (prolonged use lightens the body, brightens the eyes); the finder excluded it, and I confirm the excluded text exists and that its removal does not alter the sense of what remains.

Almost nothing in it is citable clinical content.

SAFETY GAP, and it is the most consequential thing in the source. Culpeper's one substantive internal use is parturient, with an explicit abortifacient warning and a dose ceiling: 'Let them not take above half a dram of it at a time in powder, and be sure also the birth be ripe, else it causes abortion.' I separately confirmed the finder's counter-evidence: at line 2949 the Stanyajanana (galactiphorous) decad reads 'Virana (a), Sali (b), Shastika (c), Ikshuvalika (d), the roots of Darbha (e), of Kuga (f), and of Kaga (g), Gundra (h), and the roots of Itkata (i), and of Kattrina (j), — these ten are Stanyajanana or glactiphorous.23' — Shatavari/Atirasa is absent.
results.supportsTheClaim: The passage underwrites exactly one thing: that Charaka lists this drug, under the synonym Atirasa, among the ten Valya (invigorating/strengthening) drugs. That is a classification of ACTION only. It assigns no taste, no temperature, no moisture. It therefore does NOT support taste 'Sweet, Bitter', does NOT support temperature 'Cool', does NOT support moisture 'Moist', and does NOT support 'cools deficient and Pitta heat' — the Sanskrit-medicine rasa/virya/vipaka properties are simply not present anywhere in this chapter, which is a bare enumeration of 500 drugs into 50 decads. On 'promotes breast milk' the cited work is not merely silent but actively adverse: the milk-producing decad is ten grasses, reeds and rices and does not contain this plant.
concerns: The excerpt is genuine but the STORED citation is not what I verified. The stored work field is 'Charaka Samhita (classical Ayurvedic compendium), bundled with The Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India' with year 'classical' and a locator that is a prose restatement of the title. Nothing in the stored citation names a translation, a sthana, a chapter or a page. The locator I could resolve is one the finder reconstructed. As stored, the citation is unfalsifiable and should not ship in that form.

The year field 'classical' is not a date and cannot be tested against the 1899 cutoff. The edition that actually carries this text is Kaviratna 1890-1908, which straddles the cutoff — the Sutrasthana volume containing p.32 is the early (1890s) part, but the item as a whole runs to 1908.

The citation bundles The Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, a modern work on the forbidden list for energetics support. One citation naming two works, one eligible and one not, is precisely the disguise pattern this review exists to catch. The two must be split.

NEW FINDING the finder did not raise: the identification Atirasa = Asparagus racemosus is not stable even within this single translation. At the vayahsthapana (anti-ageing) decad on printed page 47 (line 3819), Kaviratna footnotes the same name Atirasa as 'A variety of Rasna. Some physicians use Anantamula (Hemidesmus Indica) for Atirasa.' The species anchoring for this row rests entirely on one translator's footnote in one decad, and that translator contradicts himself fifteen pages later. The Sanskrit text itself never says Asparagus racemosus.

Minor correction to the finder: the Stanyajanana decad is on printed page 36, not 37. The book's own cross-reference at line 70575 reads 'Vide p. 36'. The substance of the finder's point is confirmed.

'Verified in archive.org item BIUSante_47357' is an OCR layer, not the printed page. The text is legible enough here to be conclusive, but the source of record is an OCR transcription and the citation should say so.

results.whatIFound: Downloaded henriettes-herb.com/eclectic/kings/cassia.html and stripped to text. I also confirmed the Specific Indications line in full: 'Wind or bilious colics; a laxative for non-inflammatory conditions of the intestinal tract.' And the Alexandria-senna taste sentence: 'an unpleasant, nauseous, mucilaginous, and sweetish taste, with hardly any perceptible bitterness, unless it be admixed with the leaves of the Argel'.
results.supportsTheClaim: It genuinely supports the cathartic action, the site of action (small intestines, augmented mucous secretion, increased peristalsis) and the contraindication list. It does NOT support temperature=Cold — it denies a refrigerant action in the same breath and asserts a slight stimulating influence, which in Eclectic vocabulary points the opposite way. King's assigns no temperature grade to senna anywhere in the entry. It does NOT support a heat-bound-bowel indication; the Specific Indications restrict it to NON-inflammatory conditions. It does NOT support 'habit-forming'; the entry states the contrary outright.
concerns: THE QUOTED FRAGMENTS ARE OUT OF SOURCE ORDER. 'Constipation does not follow its employment.' is placed last in the excerpt, behind three '[...]' markers, but in King's it appears EARLIER than the small-intestines sentence and the refrigerant sentence. Elision marks imply forward-only omission; here they conceal a reordering. The reordering does not change the meaning, but a quotation presented as sequential is not sequential.

THE 'SAID TO SUPPORT' OVERREACHES THE QUOTED TEXT. It claims the excerpt supports 'the griping/flatulence caveat'. The griping sentence — 'very few persons can use it alone, without experiencing more or less griping pains and flatulence' — is real and is in the entry, but it is NOT inside the quoted excerpt. As written, the excerpt does not carry that caveat and cannot be cited for it.

TASTE=BITTER IS INTERNALLY CONTESTED WITHIN THE ONE ENTRY, in a way that cuts both directions. King's own prose says Alexandria senna has 'hardly any perceptible bitterness' and attributes bitterness to the ARGEL adulterant. But the U.S.P. description King's reproduces in the same section says Alexandria senna has 'a nauseous, bitter taste', and India senna 'taste mucilaginous, bitter, and nauseous'. Whichever way the row goes, it must not cite this entry as though it spoke with one voice.

I confirm the three direct contradictions the finder raised (temperature=Cold, heat-bound-bowel indication, habit-forming). All three are contradicted by the row's OWN cited primary, which is the worst possible configuration: an eligible pre-1900 source cited in support of fields it refutes.

results.supportsTheClaim: The SNBCJ line supports taste=Pungent (辛) and temperature=Warm (溫) for the drug as that text defines it, and supports 胸中瘕熱逆氣 and 利水谷 as indications. It does NOT support moisture=Dry; 'by implication' is an inference by the finder, not a statement of the source. It does not support the aging doctrine, the Guangchenpi/Xinhui provenance, or any organ-system framing.
concerns: I CONFIRM AND SHARPEN THE COMPOUND-HEADING PROBLEM, and it is worse than the finder allowed. 橘柚 covers two fruits, and the row's herb is only the first. The gloss 一名橘皮 partially rescues it — but Li Shizhen, in the very BCGM passage the citation cross-checks against, explicitly splits them on temperature: '橘皮性温柑柚皮性冷' (mandarin peel is warm, tangerine-orange and pomelo peel are cold). So on the cross-check source's own reasoning, the 溫 of a heading that yokes 橘 and 柚 together cannot be transferred cleanly to the row's plant. BCGM 卷30 also relays 宗奭's complaint that '本草橘柚作一條盖傳誤也' — that the Bencao's joining of them into one entry is a transmission error that caused people to mistake pomelo peel for mandarin peel.

The row has silently merged two sources: it reproduces BCGM's 苦辛溫 while attributing the 主治 string to 本經. BCGM itself keeps the two apart — it prints its own 氣味 line and only then marks the 主治 clause {本經}. The row does not.

The aging premise (part_used, herb name, 'aging mellows the volatile oils') is entirely absent from the cited Han text. It IS attestable pre-1900 from Tao Hongjing via BCGM — I verified 「橘皮療氣大勝，以東橘為好，西江者不如，須陳久者為良」 verbatim at offset 22395 — but that is a different work, a different century, and it is not the citation as stored.

WORLDVIEW: the omitted clause 久服，去臭、下氣、通神 ends in 通神. The finder correctly excluded it and the quoted portion is clean. Note that BCGM reproduces the same clause including 通神, so any expansion of this excerpt from the BCGM side would reintroduce it.

SUSPICIOUS-EXACTNESS CHECK, AND A SPECIES CAVEAT THE FINDER MISSED. The quoted taste phrase matching the stored value exactly does survive scrutiny — it is a U.S.P. description quoted inside King's, marked with quotation marks and attributed. results.supportsTheClaim: Culpeper genuinely supports temperature=Warm and moisture=Dry ('hot and dry in the third degree'), plus anthelmintic, emmenagogue and antidotal indications. Grieve genuinely supports the action list and the preparations, but Grieve assigns NO temperature, NO taste and NO moisture — I read the entire entry and the words hot, warm, cold, cool and bitter (of the herb) do not appear as energetic gradings. NEITHER source supports the row's taste field.
concerns: THE LINE NUMBERS IN THE LOCATOR DO NOT MATCH THE CANONICAL GUTENBERG FILE. Claimed 16129 / 18603 / 18645 / 18807 / 18817; in gutenberg.org/files/49513/49513-0.txt they are 16099 / 18573 / 18615 / 18777 / 18787 — a uniform 30-line offset, which is the length of the boilerplate header the current file no longer carries. The content resolves; the numbers do not. Line numbers into a Gutenberg plain-text file are a fragile locator and should be replaced with the section name plus entry heading, which is stable.

THE PRIMARY/SECONDARY SLOTS ARE INVERTED, and this is the substantive defect. Grieve (1931) is in the primary slot and is post-1900 and silent on all three energetics fields. The only pre-1900 evidence for Warm and Dry — the Culpeper line — sits in the secondary slot.

'A hot, dry herb of Mercury' is half-invented. 'Hot and dry' is verbatim. 'Of Mercury' is not: I verified there is no Southernwood chapter in the Complete Herbal at all, hence no 'Government and virtues' paragraph, hence no planetary assignment. Culpeper does write 'It is an herb of Mercury' for other plants (I found eight such lines), which is how a plausible-sounding attribution gets manufactured. It must not ship.
Even if it existed, planetary rulership is astrological framing and is excluded by the worldview filter.

The Dioscorides attribution reaches the row second-hand. In Grieve's page the Dioscorides material sits inside a block quotation headed 'Culpepper says:' which opens 'Dioscorides saith that the seed bruised...'. Citing De Materia Medica directly, as the secondary citation does, misrepresents a quote-within-a-quote as a first-hand consultation.

PROVENANCE NOTE: the 'A Brotanum' entry is not in the herbal proper but in the appended catalogue of simples that the standard combined editions carry. The locator states this correctly, so this is disclosure rather than a defect — but the '1653' year attaches to the herbal, and the catalogue's own publication history differs.

The 'narcotic alkaloid' attribution for the acrid taste is not what King's says. The entry also relays Prof. Maisch's suspicion 'that the virtues ascribed to spigelia might, in reality, be those of phlox, since this root has long been used in the southern states.' Any strong efficacy language sourced to this entry inherits that doubt, and the row's summary does not reflect it.

The entry (offset 62554) reads: '==桔梗== 味辛，微溫。主胸脅痛如刀刺，腹滿，腸鳴幽幽，驚恐悸氣（《御覽》引云：一名利如。《大觀本》作黑字）。生山谷。' followed by '《吳普》曰：桔梗，一名符扈，一名白芍，一名利如，一名梗草，一名盧如。神農、醫和：苦，無毒；扁鵲、黃帝：咸；岐伯、雷公：甘，無毒；李氏：大寒。葉如薺…'. The section head at offset 58836 reads '= 卷三·下經 = 下藥，一百二十五種，為左使。主治病以應地。多毒，不可久服。欲除寒熱邪氣，破積聚，愈疾者，本下經。' — the claimed head '下藥，一百二十五種，為左使……多毒，不可久服。' is verbatim with the ellipsis correctly covering 主治病以應地。I verified the grade THREE independent ways, as the finder did: (1) 桔梗 appears in the 下品 index line inside 卷三·下經, between 葶藶 and 莨蕩子, in the block closing '（上草，下品四十九種。舊四十八種）'; (2) a substring test over the entire 卷二·中經 span returns FALSE for 桔梗; (3) the compatibility tables list it under '==草藥，下部==' ('桔梗　節皮為使；畏白芨；反龍膽、龍眼'). I also confirmed 咳 does not appear in the entry.
results.supportsTheClaim: It supports taste=Pungent (辛) and the indications 胸脅痛如刀刺 and 腹滿. It CONTRADICTS the row's temperature=Neutral: the text reads 微溫, slightly warm. 'Bitter' is not in the main line — 苦 appears only inside the 吳普 doxography as one of several mutually incompatible school attributions (神農/醫和 say 苦, 扁鵲/黃帝 say 咸, 岐伯/雷公 say 甘, 李氏 says 大寒), which is a record of DISAGREEMENT and cannot be cited as the source's position on anything. It supports none of the row's stated actions: no phlegm, no pus, no Lung, no upward-floating messenger.
concerns: UNMARKED ELISION IN THE EXCERPT. The claimed text runs '…驚恐悸氣。生山谷。' but the source interposes an editorial parenthetical: '驚恐悸氣（《御覽》引云：一名利如。《大觀本》作黑字）。生山谷。'. The omission is of a collation note, not of substance, but it is presented as continuous text with no ellipsis. Every other elision in this batch is marked; this one is not.

GRADE ERROR CONFIRMED. The citation asserts middle-grade (中品). It is LOWER grade (下品), under a section heading that reads 多毒，不可久服 — 'mostly toxic, not to be taken for long'. This is not a nuance: it inverts the safety framing the citation implies.

'COUGH' IS NOT IN THE ENTRY. Confirmed: 咳 does not occur. The remaining indications are 腸鳴幽幽 (faint bowel rumbling) and 驚恐悸氣 (fright, fear, palpitation) — neither is respiratory. The citation's claim that the source records it for cough is fabricated detail attached to a real passage, which is the hardest kind to catch.

TEMPERATURE CONTRADICTED: the row stores Neutral; the source states 微溫. Note this row does NOT trip the suspicious-exactness rule — the source disagrees with the stored value, which is the honest direction for a genuine excerpt to fail in.

The 吳普 doxography should not be surfaced as supporting evidence for any taste or temperature. It records four schools disagreeing and a fifth (李氏) calling it 大寒, very cold — the polar opposite of the main line's 微溫. Quoting it selectively could support almost any value.

results.whatIFound: I downloaded my own copy of 神農本草經 (孫星衍) raw wikitext (242,119 bytes, matching the size the finder reported) and grepped it. At line 258 the file carries the heading ==干地黃== and at line 260 the body reads, character for character: 「味甘，寒。主折跌絕筋，傷中，逐血痹，填骨髓，長肌肉，作湯，除寒熱積聚，除痹，生者尤良。久服，輕身、不老。一名地髓。生川澤。」 An exact-string count of the excerpt body returns 1. The string 熟地黃 returns 0 occurrences in the entire Shennong Bencao Jing, confirming the finder's negative claim. I separately downloaded 本草綱目 (四庫全書本)/卷16 (175,019 bytes) and confirmed the cross-reference: 「熟地黄　修治…氣味甘微苦微温無毒」 is present, as are 「蒸乾即温補生乾即平宣」 and 「鮮用則寒乾用則凉」 (the Siku text uses the glyph variants 温/凉, not 溫/涼).
results.supportsTheClaim: The passage genuinely supports taste Sweet (味甘) and temperature Cold (寒) for the dried/raw root 干地黃, and supports 填骨髓，長肌肉. It does NOT support Warm, does NOT support 'Slightly bitter', and does NOT support the prepared 熟地黃 form in any way, since that term is wholly absent from the work. I verified all three negatives by exact string count.
concerns: EXACT-MATCH RED FLAG, CONFIRMED INDEPENDENTLY BY ME. The row's stored taste 'Sweet, Slightly bitter' and temperature 'Warm' are a character-for-character match to Bencao Gangmu 卷16 熟地黄 「氣味甘微苦微温無毒」, a DIFFERENT work from the one cited. I confirmed this string exists in my own download of BCGM 卷16. This is the same shape as the withdrawn Lion's Mane citation: the row's stored values reproduce a source that is not the source named.

The excerpt string as presented joins the section heading 干地黃 to the body with a full-width space. In the source these are on separate lines (a == == wiki heading and a body paragraph). An exact search for '干地黃　味甘' returns 0. This is a presentation artifact rather than fabrication, but the excerpt as stored is not a contiguous run of source characters.

The excerpt stops at 生者尤良。 with no ellipsis, silently dropping 「久服，輕身、不老。一名地髓。生川澤。」 The finder discloses this truncation in the concerns and gives a worldview-filter reason for it, which is honest, but the excerpt string itself carries no elision mark.

The cited work bundles 'Bensky, Clavey & Stoger', which the finder notes is on the forbidden list. The citation therefore names two works at once, one of them disallowed, which is the multi-work shape that produced earlier withdrawals.
The correct pre-1900 support for this row's actual stored values is BCGM 卷16, not the Shennong Bencao Jing. As cited, the source and the stored energetics do not match.

The first block sits in the U.S.P. description; the second in 'Action, Medical Uses, and Dosage'. The entry header reads 'The bark of Rhamnus Purshiana, De Candolle (Rhamnus alnifolius, Pursh; Frangula Purshiana, Cooper).' Case-insensitive counts across the whole entry: 'astringen' = 0, 'cool' = 0, 'one year' = 0.
results.supportsTheClaim: Supports Bitter directly ('inodorous; taste bitter', quoted from the U.S.P.) and supports the intestinal-tonic action claim verbatim. It does NOT support Cool: the word does not occur anywhere in the entry, and King's assigns no humoral temperature to this drug. It does NOT support Dry. It does NOT support Astringent: 'astringen' has zero occurrences in the entry; the only tannin reference is 'a tannic acid' in the constituents list, which is a chemical finding, not a taste statement.
concerns: Cool and Dry have no textual basis whatever in the cited work. I confirmed zero occurrences of 'cool' in the entry. An Eclectic dispensatory structurally cannot carry a humoral temperature, so no amount of correct quotation from King's will ever underwrite that field.
Astringent is back-inferred from chemistry. Confirmed: King's never calls this bark astringent anywhere in the entry.

The row's 'aged at least one year' rule is not in King's. I searched for 'one year' and got zero hits. What King's actually says is about a ferment 'occurring especially in recent bark, and being destroyed by heat' (verified verbatim), which is a narrower and different claim.

Minor: the entry title is rendered on the page as 'Rhamnus Purshiana (U. S. P.)—Cascara Sagrada.' The citation writes it with spaced dashes. Trivial, but note the working slug really is 'rhamnus-purs'.

S. P.); (3) in 'Action, Medical Uses, and Dosage' — 'The carminative, antispasmodic, and stimulant properties of spearmint are somewhat inferior to those of peppermint; its principal employment is for its diuretic and febrifuge virtues. As a febrifuge, it is superior to peppermint, and may be used freely in warm infusion.'; (4) 'Specific Indications and Uses.—Scanty secretion of urine with frequent desire to urinate; simple nausea.' The page's botanical name tag is Mentha spicata; the header is 'The leaves and tops of Mentha viridis, Linné'—(U. S. P.), with (Mentha sylvestris, var. glabra, Koch.). Correct species and correct part. I also fetched the Grieve page separately for H234 and note that this entry contains the sentence 'It contains a little tannin.'
results.supportsTheClaim: Supports Pungent (U.S.P. 'taste pungent') and the faintly bitter note, and supports the carminative/antispasmodic action and the 'simple nausea' indication verbatim. It does NOT support Cool as a humoral temperature — see concerns. It does NOT support Dry and does NOT support a Sweet taste component; neither appears anywhere in the entry.
concerns: I DISAGREE WITH THE FINDER ON 'COOL'. The finder writes that the entry supports Cool 'indirectly and reasonably well'. It does not. 'Followed by coolness in the mouth during inhalation' is a description of a transient oral sensation in the History/Chemistry section, not a thermal grading of the drug, and 'As a febrifuge, it is superior to peppermint' is a therapeutic indication, not a temperature. King's assigns no humoral temperature anywhere in this entry. Chaining a mouth sensation plus a febrifuge use into a Cool grading is inference by the finder, not support from the source, and should be labelled as unsupported the same way Dry and Sweet are.
The stored url is the bare corpus directory /eclectic/kings/, not the entry page. As stored the citation is not re-findable without searching. Confirmed by the finder and I concur.
The locator field repeats the title string and gives no section pointer. That is the same unverifiable shape as the four previously withdrawn citations.
The citation names Grieve (1931) as corroboration inside the same record. Post-1900, cannot carry taste or temperature. Naming two works in one citation is itself one of the recurring failure shapes.

'It contains a little tannin' does appear in this entry. If anyone later reaches for that to justify an astringency claim, note that King's never calls spearmint astringent — same constituent-versus-taste error as H129.

results.whatIFound: In my own download of 神農本草經 (孫星衍), line 578 gives ==黃連== and line 580 reads: 「味苦，寒。主熱氣目痛、　傷泣出，明目（《御覽》引云：主莖傷。《大觀本》無），腸，腹痛下利，婦人陰中腫痛。久服，令人不忘。一名王連。生川谷。」 The two corruptions the finder flagged are real and reproduce in my independent copy: a blank box where 眥 should stand, and 澼 dropped after 腸. I then downloaded 本草綱目 (四庫全書本)/卷13 myself (118,438 bytes) and confirmed the restorations: it carries 「主治熱氣目痛眥傷泣出明目腸澼腹痛下痢婦人隂中腫痛」 (exact count 1) and 「氣味苦寒無毒」 (count 4 in the juan). I also confirmed the finder's Dry-attribution notes in BCGM 卷13: 「好古曰黄連苦燥」 and 「苦能燥濕寒能勝熱」 both present. Within the Huang Lian entry of the SNBCJ itself, 燥 = 0 occurrences and 濕 = 0.
results.supportsTheClaim: Supports taste Bitter (苦) and temperature Cold (寒) directly and unaltered — that clause is untouched by either corruption, so the energetics rest on clean text. Supports the intestinal-flux/abdominal-pain/dysentery indication. Confirms superior-class listing (黃連 appears in the 草上品 index at line 36 of the file). It does NOT support moisture=Dry, does NOT support the Heart-fire framing, and does NOT support any species identification more precise than 'huang lian'.
concerns: ONE UNDISCLOSED ELISION INSIDE THE QUOTATION MARKS. The finder discloses and brackets both emendations (眥, 澼), which is correct scholarly practice and which I independently corroborated against BCGM 卷13. But the excerpt also silently drops the editorial parenthetical 「（《御覽》引云：主莖傷。《大觀本》無）」 after 明目, with no ellipsis. The excerpt string therefore does not appear contiguously in the source. This is a defect of presentation, not of substance, but it should be marked before the text is written.

With three edits inside one quoted run (two bracketed insertions plus one unmarked deletion), the excerpt is a critical reconstruction, not a transcription. If the database stores it as a verbatim quotation it will be storing something no printed witness carries in exactly that form. Store the raw wikisource string and put the emendations in a note, or mark the elision.

The finder pre-empts the exact-match suspicion and I checked it rather than accepting the reassurance: Bitter/Cold is confirmed from two independently downloaded texts of different date (SNBCJ 1799 recension and BCGM 卷13). I agree this is not a Lion's-Mane-shaped coincidence.
moisture=Dry is genuinely absent from the cited work. I confirmed 燥 = 0 in the SNBCJ entry. If Dry is to stand it must be recited to BCGM 卷13 發明, where I verified 「好古曰黄連苦燥」 and 「苦能燥濕寒能勝熱」 do exist.

The 張元素 'quenching Heart fire' line the finder quotes as 「瀉心臟火一也，去中焦濕熱二也」 does not appear in BCGM 卷13 in that exact form; my copy reads 「…火一也去中焦濕熱二也諸瘡必用三也…」 with 瀉心火, not 瀉心臟火. This is only in a concern note, not in the excerpt, but do not carry that string forward as a quotation.
A Han-dynasty text cannot underwrite a modern binomial. Coptis chinensis is a later identification, not something the SNBCJ states.

It is a favorite remedy in prolonged insomnia, particularly in the aged, and in those of an excessively nervous temperament.'; 'Beside the active principle, piscidia (piscidin), some resin, caoutchouc, wax and fat, starch (1.34 per cent), were present; tannin was not found.' (my first exact match failed only because of italic-tag whitespace around 'piscidin'; the run is verbatim); and 'Piscidia destroys life by causing heart failure or by arresting respiratory action.' Whole-entry counts: 'sweet' = 0, 'cool' = 0. The header reads 'The bark of the root of Piscidia Erythrina, Jacquin.' with the page's botanical-name tag Piscidia piscipula.
results.supportsTheClaim: Supports the taste (acrid and bitter), the whole indication set (pain, spasm, nervous excitability, insomnia, neuralgia/sciatica/migraine), the toxicity profile and the narrow margin. It does NOT support Cool: zero occurrences of 'cool' in the entry, and King's assigns no thermal quality. It does NOT support any sweetish note: zero occurrences of 'sweet' in the entire entry, which affirmatively refutes the row's taste field rather than merely failing to confirm it.
concerns: Temperature 'Cool' has no basis in the cited work. Confirmed by me: zero hits.

The row's 'faint sweetish, slightly aromatic note' is affirmatively contradicted. The string 'sweet' does not occur once in the entry. The finder is right that this reads like contamination from a neighbouring row.

PART MISMATCH IN THE ASTRINGENCY EVIDENCE, WHICH THE FINDER DID NOT NAME AS SUCH. King's defines the drug as 'The bark of the ROOT of Piscidia Erythrina, Jacquin', and its 'Description' section describes root bark. But the sentence 'The bark of the tree is very astringent, and is said to have been used in tanning' sits in 'Botanical Source and History' and describes the bark of the TREE, i.e. a different part from the official drug. Any astringency claim resting on that line is resting on the wrong plant part, on top of being contradicted by the analysis of the actual drug ('tannin was not found').
The stored locator merely restates the title and the stored url points at the King's corpus index, not the entry. Not re-findable as stored.

Latin-name note: King's treats the drug as Piscidia Erythrina, Jacquin; the row stores Piscidia piscipula. Accepted synonyms, so not a species error, but the citation should record which name the 1898 text uses.

results.whatIFound: I downloaded Gutenberg ebook 49513 myself (1,531,341 bytes) and read the passages directly. Line 11588 is the chapter heading 'WINTER AND SUMMER SAVOURY.' and lines 11596-11603 carry, verbatim: 'They are both of them hot and dry, especially the Summer kind, which is both sharp and quick in taste, expelling wind in the stomach and bowels, and is a present help for the rising of the mother procured by wind; provokes urine and women's courses, and is much commended...' and 'It cures tough phlegm in the chest and lungs, and helps to expectorate it the more easily;'. Line 17245 reads verbatim: '_Satureia._ Savory. Summer savory is hot and dry in the third degree, Winter savory is not so hot, both of them expel wind.' Line 18609 lists under '_In the third degree._' ... 'summer and winter Savory'. The dry-in-the-third-degree table (around line 18650) lists 'winter and summer Savory'. The index confirms p.166: 'Savine, 166 / Savory, Winter and Summer, ib.' For Grieve I fetched botanical.com/botanical/mgmh/s/savsum24.html directly; a plain curl got HTTP 406, a browser User-Agent got HTTP 200. The page is titled 'A Modern Herbal | Savory, Summer', botanical name Satureia hortensis (LINN.), and its '---Medicinal Action and Uses---' section carries the quoted sentences verbatim. 'astringent' returns zero occurrences in the Grieve page and the Culpeper savory chapter contains no astringency, binding or bowel-tightening language.
results.supportsTheClaim: Culpeper genuinely supports Warm and Dry, the pungent taste ('sharp and quick in taste'), the carminative action, the emmenagogue action and the expectorant use. Grieve supports aromatic/carminative/warming/expectorant but assigns no temperature, no taste and no moisture, and is post-1900 in any case. NEITHER source supports the row's astringency or the 'tightens a loose, lax bowel' indication — I searched both and found nothing.
concerns: THE FINDER'S FACTUAL-ERROR FLAG IS CORRECT AND I CONFIRM IT AT THREE PLACES. The row says 'hot and dry in the second degree'. Culpeper's catalogue of simples (line 17245) says THIRD degree, his hot-in-the-third-degree table (line 18609) lists summer savory, and his dry-in-the-third-degree table (line ~18650) lists it again. The row contradicts the source it names, three times over.

THE CITATION RECORD IS MALFORMED IN EXACTLY THE WAY THAT PRODUCED EARLIER WITHDRAWALS. The cited work is Grieve (1931), the year field reads 1931, and Grieve carries none of the energetics. The only work that actually carries temperature, moisture and taste is Culpeper 1653, which is named only inside the primary citation's free-text title. That is both the 'year field disguising the source' shape and the 'one citation naming several works at once' shape. This should be split into a Culpeper 1653 citation carrying the energetics and, if wanted at all, a separate Grieve entry restricted to indications.
The row's 'distinct astringency' and 'tightens a loose, lax bowel' are unsupported by either cited text. I independently searched both for astringent/binding/flux/looseness/diarrhoea and found zero.

'Mercury claims dominion over this herb' is astrological and excluded by the worldview filter. The usable observations ('hot and dry', 'sharp and quick in taste', 'expelling wind') stand without it. Note Grieve quotes the same Mercury line, so it will resurface if the Grieve page is used uncritically.
Minor locator drift: the dry-in-the-third-degree line is at 18651 in my copy, not 18650. Off by one, harmless.

Note that Culpeper's chapter treats winter and summer savory together and the chapter itself says only 'hot and dry' without a degree; the degree comes from the catalogue and the tables. Any citation should point at the catalogue/table lines, not the chapter, for the degree.

results.whatIFound: I fetched https://www.henriettes-herb.com/eclectic/kings/phytolacca.html myself (HTTP 200, 36,993 bytes). (my first exact match failed only on italic-tag whitespace in 'The root ,'); 'The young, green shoots, as they start in the spring and before the leaves have developed, are used as a table vegetable, being considered the best substitute for asparagus.'; 'They become cathartic as they advance to maturity.'; 'The berries steeped in gin have long been popular as a remedy for chronic rheumatism.'; the Description heading 'II. PHYTOLACCAE RADIX (U. S. P.), Poke-root.' followed by the U.S.P. text 'Large, conical, branched and fleshy; ... fracture fibrous, the wood-bundles in several distinct, concentric circles; inodorous; taste sweetish and acrid'—(U. S. P.); 'Therapeutically, phytolacca is emetic, cathartic, narcotic, and alterative.'; and the glandular/mastitis/tonsillitis run. results.supportsTheClaim: Supports, very fully and verbatim: root as principal drug, autumn harvest, the berry-in-gin rheumatism use, poke sallet as spring shoots, the alterative/glandular/lymphatic indication set including mastitis and tonsillitis, and the toxic margin (I confirmed 'It is a paralyzer of the spinal cord' and 'Death results from carbonic acid poisoning, the result of respiratory paralysis'). It does NOT support Cool (zero occurrences), does NOT support Bitter as a taste, and affirmatively CONTRADICTS Astringent.
concerns: THE STORED TASTE IS CONTRADICTED BY THE SOURCE AND I CONFIRM IT. King's, quoting the U.S.P., gives the root 'taste sweetish and acrid' and the berry 'taste sweet, slightly acrid'. Acrid is confirmed; the source pairs it with SWEETISH, not with bitter. The word 'bitter' occurs exactly once in the whole entry and it is 'bitter resin' in a constituent list. The row's 'Bitter' has no taste-statement support here at all.

THE ASTRINGENT EDGE IS AFFIRMATIVELY REFUTED, NOT MERELY UNSUPPORTED. 'astringen' returns zero occurrences in the entry, and the quantitative analysis explicitly affirms 'the absence of tannin'. This is stronger than silence: the cited source says the opposite of the row.

Temperature 'Cool' is not in King's. Zero hits for 'cool'. The row's own temperature paragraph admits it is 'read across the modern Western tradition', which is honest but means the grading rests on post-1900 authors and cannot be attributed to this citation.

Latin-name divergence, benign: King's treats the drug as Phytolacca decandra Linné; the row stores Phytolacca americana. Accepted synonyms. The page's own botanical-name tags list P. acinosa, P. americana and P. dioica, so the tag list is not itself a species assertion by King's.

Analyst attribution: the tannin-absence analysis is by G. F. Frankforter (Amer. Jour. Pharm., 1897, p. 281). The entry also cites a G. B. Frankforter a few lines earlier. If the initials are recorded, use G. F. for the quantitative analysis.

results.supportsTheClaim: Supports all three tastes directly and verbatim: King's gives 'a pungent, peculiar, spicy odor, a bitter taste succeeded by astringency, acridity'; Thomson adds 'very pungent'. Supports the astringent-stimulant indication set (catarrhal states, atonic diarrhoea, typhoid dysentery, sore mouth, spongy bleeding gums) and the Thomsonian Composition Powder link. DOES NOT SUPPORT a temperature. Neither text contains 'warm', 'hot', 'cold' or any equivalent as an attribute of the drug. 'Warm' is an inference from 'astringent and stimulant', 'a decided gastric stimulant', 'atony of the cutaneous circulation' and Thomson's 'highly stimulating'. If the row publishes Warm as sourced to King's or Thomson, that is a claim neither work makes.
concerns: Temperature Warm has no textual basis in either cited work. I confirm the finder's flag independently: I searched both full texts and neither assigns a thermal quality to bayberry.

The stored url points at the King's index rather than /eclectic/kings/myrica.html, and the Thomson half of the citation carries no url, edition, page or archive identifier. As stored, a reader cannot follow either half; I had to locate the 1822 edition myself.

OCR defects inside the quoted Thomson passage: 'exceiient' (excellent) and 'advanlaffe' (advantage). The finder bracketed both, which is correct practice. Note the finder did NOT flag a third: the printed heading is rendered by the OCR as 'Bayberry ; or Candleeerry.' The claimed heading 'Bayberry; or Candleberry' is a silent normalisation. It is almost certainly what the page prints, but it was not read from a clean scan.

The King's excerpt splices three separate sections (History and Description, Action/Medical Uses/Dosage, Specific Indications) into one quotation string joined by ellipses. Genuine, but a reader could mistake it for continuous text.
Thomson (1822) is a pre-1900 source that describes ACTION only. It cannot carry a temperature field however real the quote.

results.whatIFound: I downloaded the Sun Xingyan (1799) recension of the Shennong Bencao Jing from zh.wikisource (raw wikitext, 242,119 bytes / 84,443 chars) and searched it. 何首烏 returns ZERO occurrences; even the bare 首烏 returns zero. The work named in the citation's author field, at the century named in its year field, does not contain this herb at all. Separately I downloaded 本草綱目 (四庫全書本)/卷18上 (108,024 bytes / 44,903 chars; the bare 卷18 page is indeed only a table of contents) and found the passage exactly. Verbatim counts, each exactly 1: 氣味苦濇微溫無毒 ; 主治瘰癧消癰腫療頭面風瘡治五痔止心痛益血氣黑髭髮悦顔色久服長筋骨益精髓延年不老亦治婦人産後及帶下諸疾. The entry is tagged {{SK notes|宋開寶}} — Li Shizhen himself sources it to the Song Kaibao Bencao, not to Shennong. I also confirmed the two secondary readings the finder raised: 何首烏味甘性溫無毒 occurs once, inside the 何首烏傳 legend quoted in 集解; and 發明 opens 何首烏足厥隂少隂藥也, exactly once.
results.supportsTheClaim: The passage genuinely supports Bitter, Astringent and slightly Warm (苦濇微溫), non-toxicity, and 黑髭髮 (blackens the moustache and hair). It does NOT support 'Sweet' — sweet appears only in the embedded Tang-era legend text, not in Li Shizhen's own 氣味 line. It does NOT support any raw-versus-prepared temperature split: the nine-steam/nine-sun black-soybean method is described in 根修治 with no reassignment of qi or wei. And critically, the passage supports nothing at all under the author and year the citation actually states, because that work does not contain the herb.
concerns: VERIFIED FALSE ATTRIBUTION. The author field (Shennong Ben Cao Jing) and year field (c. 200 CE) name a work I searched in full and which contains no He Shou Wu entry. This is the exact shape of citations this project has already withdrawn: one citation naming several works, with author and year describing a different book from title and locator. The passage is real; the citation of record is not.
The title string is internally inconsistent as well — it carries 1596 inside the title while the year field says c. 200 CE.

'Sweet' is recoverable only from 何首烏味甘性溫無毒 inside the 何首烏傳, a folk biography about a man said to have lived to 160 and fathered children at 58. Citing that as a taste authority means citing a legend, and it sits in a different structural layer (集解) from the 氣味 line.
'Rebuilds Liver Blood and Kidney essence' rests on 發明's 何首烏足厥隂少隂藥也, an explicit Foot Jueyin / Shaoyin channel attribution. That is 歸經 doctrine and is excluded by the worldview filter.
The recovered passage genuinely contradicts part of the row: Li Shizhen gives one qi-wei, 微溫 (slightly warm), for the drug as such.

results.whatIFound: First I independently confirmed the finder's URL claim: I downloaded https://www.henriettes-herb.com/eclectic/kings/cinchona-prep.html (HTTP 200). Its title is literally 'Cinchona wossname, thingy.' and it carries Henriette's note that she is not scanning the Cinchona entry. The cited page cannot have supplied this excerpt. I then downloaded archive.org kingsamericandis01kinguoft_djvu.txt (5,056,376 bytes; title page reads NINETEENTH EDITION. THIRD REVISION, Ohio Valley Company, 1905 printing). Every quoted fragment is present exactly once: 'Cinchona bark is tonic, antiperiodic, slightly astringent, and topically antise[p]tic'; 'When swallowed, a sensation of warmth is experienced at the stomach, which gradually spreads over the whole trunk'; 'Cinchona is valuable in functional derangement of the stomach...'; 'exhibits its most important therapeutical powers as an antiperiodic'; 'Cinchona is to be preferred when an astringent effect is desired'; 'Its employment is contraindicated in acute inflammation'; 'weakness, with pale surface, loss of appetite, feeble digestion, and deficient recuperative powers'; 'with scarcely any astringency'; and 'powder reddish-brown; odor slight; taste bitter and astringent'. Page markers confirm the locator: 'CINCHONA. 551' immediately precedes 'Action, Medical Uses, and Dosage', '552 CINCHONA' falls mid-paragraph, and Specific Indications is on 552. BUT the U.S.P. taste fragment is misassigned. The monograph splits the drug into two official classes. Class I, 'CINCHONA (U.S.P.)', is defined as 'The bark of Cinchona Calisaya, Weddell; Cinchona officinalis, Linné; and of hybrids' and reads 'powder light-brown or yellowish-brown; odor slight, somewhat aromatic; taste bitter and SOMEWHAT astringent'. Class II, 'CINCHONA RUBRA (U.S.P.)', is 'The bark of Cinchona succirubra, Pavon' and is the one that reads 'powder reddish-brown; odor slight; taste bitter and astringent'. The excerpt quotes the succirubra description for a row about C. officinalis.
results.supportsTheClaim: The Action/Medical Uses material is genuine and supports the indications: intermittent and remittent fever, periodicity, loss of appetite, feeble digestion, debility, convalescence, and the contraindication in acute inflammation. It supports 'bitter'. It does NOT support 'astringent' at the strength the row implies, and the fragment used to support it is the wrong species. For C. officinalis specifically King's says 'taste bitter and somewhat astringent'; the Action section says 'slightly astringent'; and of calisaya 'with scarcely any astringency'. Above all it does NOT support temperature 'Cold'. King's is an Eclectic source and assigns no temperature; the only sensible-quality statement in the entire monograph runs the other way — 'a sensation of warmth is experienced at the stomach, which gradually spreads over the whole trunk'.
concerns: WRONG PLANT INSIDE THE RIGHT MONOGRAPH. The quoted U.S.P. taste line describes Cinchona succirubra (red cinchona), not Cinchona officinalis. The C. officinalis class hedges astringency down to 'somewhat astringent'. Dropping that hedge is precisely what inflates the row's astringent taste field. The finder did not catch this.

The stored url (henriettes-herb.com/eclectic/kings/) demonstrably does not contain the Cinchona monograph — verified by download, not inference. Whatever produced this excerpt, it was not the cited page.

The row's temperature 'Cold' is contradicted by the only warmth/coolness language in the cited work. This is the Ginkgo failure pattern: the row asserts a temperature the named source does not give, and the source's own language points the other way.

The archive.org item verified against is the 1905 Ohio Valley Company printing of the 19th ed./3rd revision, while the citation says 1898. Same revision, different impression; the year field should say which.

The bracketed OCR corrections in the claimed excerpt do not exactly track the OCR. The scan reads 'antisejitic' and 'convalesience', not the forms implied by '[p]' and '[c]'. The printed text is almost certainly as claimed, but the brackets misdescribe what was on screen.
For C. officinalis specifically (the pale/crown bark), King's rates it INFERIOR as an antiperiodic: 'the red and yellow are considered superior to the pale'.

results.herb: Phellodendron (Amur Cork Tree, Huang Bai) — Phellodendron amurense
results.whatIFound: I downloaded the Sun Xingyan Shennong Bencao Jing raw wikitext myself and searched it. The full claimed string 味苦，寒。主五臟、腸胃中結熱，黃膽，腸痔，止泄利，女子漏下赤白，陰陽蝕創，一名檀桓。生山谷。 occurs exactly once, character for character including the 黃膽 orthography. I independently reproduce the finder's transcription flag: the section header at this entry reads literally '==木==' with the 檗 glyph dropped. Identity is nailed by the entry's own 案 note, 《說文》云：檗，黃木也，...張揖云：檗木，可染者. I also verified the class placement the finder asserted but did not evidence: the header '= 卷一·上經 =' is at char 4,515 and '= 卷二·中經 =' at 37,256; the entry sits at 28,632, so it is in the Upper Class. The 上經 index block lists it in the 木上品 run between 酸棗 and 乾漆.
results.supportsTheClaim: Supports taste 苦 (bitter) and temperature 寒 (cold) exactly as recorded. Strongly supports the lower-burner damp-heat identity: 腸胃中結熱 (bound heat in intestines and stomach), 黃膽 (jaundice), 腸痔 (intestinal haemorrhoids), 止泄利 (stops diarrhoea and dysentery), 女子漏下赤白 (red and white leakage), 陰陽蝕創 (erosive sores of the genitals). It does NOT support anything about the Kidney, about empty or deficient fire, or about a Water/Fire relationship.
concerns: The stored taste and temperature match the source EXACTLY (bitter, cold). Flagging per the standing instruction to be more suspicious, not less, when an excerpt says precisely what the database already claims. My independent judgement is that this one is genuine: I retrieved the text myself from my own download, the surrounding entries (茯苓, 榆皮, 酸棗, 乾漆, 五加皮) are the expected 木上品 neighbours, and bitter-cold for Huang Bai is uncontested. But the coincidence is real and should be recorded.
'Cools the empty fire of spent Kidney water' is NOT in the cited work. Neither 腎 nor 虛火 appears anywhere in this entry. Yin-deficiency fire is a Jin-Yuan doctrine roughly twelve centuries later.

TRANSCRIPTION DEFECT IN THE SOURCE OF RECORD, confirmed twice over. The wikisource entry header has lost 檗 entirely ('==木=='), AND the 上經 index in the same file spells the herb 柏木 (cypress wood) rather than 檗木. Anyone re-checking by searching 檗木 or 黃柏 will hit almost nothing and may wrongly conclude the entry is absent. The locator must carry this emendation.
'Among the herbs for heat, dampness, and toxic sores' is a modern category heading, not a Shennong structure. The classic's own structure places it in 上經 / 木上品, which the citation does not mention.

results.herb: Vidanga / False Black Pepper (Embelia ribes Burm.f.)
results.whatIFound: BHAVAPRAKASA: I downloaded the Srikantha Murthy Krishnadas Academy 2001 edition djvu text from archive.org (1,328,026 bytes) myself. The Vidanga entry is present under the running head 'HARITAKYADI VARGA 177', headed 'Vidanga—Bot.—Embelia ribes Burm', and reads (OCR column damage restored from the stray fragment 'cr abdomen, muti' printed out of order on the same page): 'Vidanga is pungent, penetrating, hot in potency, dry (causes dryness), increases digestive fire, easily digestable, cures colic, flatulence, enlargement of the abdomen, mitigates kapha and vata, removes worms and constipation.' 'removes worms and constipation' occurs exactly once in the whole 1.3 MB file. CHARAKA: I downloaded the Kaviratna (Abinash Chandra) 1892 djvu text (1,153,811 bytes). The Sutrasthana 4 list is at the page marked 'CHARAKA-SAMIUTA, 35' and reads 'Akhira, Maricha, Gandira, Kevuka, Nirgunthi, Vidanga, Kinihi, Acwadangshtra, Vrishaparni, and Akhuparni,—these ten are Krimighna [anthelmintic]' with footnote 'Embelia Ribes' against Vidanga. Vidanga is sixth of ten and no member is singled out. The 'foremost' statement is at the page marked 'CHARAKA-SAMHITA. 279', inside Lesson XXV, and reads 'Of all things used as amthelmintics, the foremost are Vidanga (the seeds of Limbelia Ribes, ; syn, E. glandulifera)' — 'amthelmintics' and 'Limbelia' are OCR errors for 'anthelmintics' and 'Embelia'.
results.supportsTheClaim: Supports taste pungent (katu), temperature warm (ushna virya — 'hot in potency' is stated outright, the only affirmative temperature in this whole batch), moisture dry ('dry (causes dryness)'), the gunas tikshna and laghu, the dipana action, kapha-and-vata reduction, and the anthelmintic indication including 'foremost'. Does NOT support astringent or bitter rasa — neither word appears in the Bhavaprakasa entry. Does NOT support the citation's own assertion that Sutrasthana 4 names Vidanga chief of the Krimighna mahakashaya; that chapter names no chief.
concerns: I confirm the finder's locator error against the text. Charaka Sutrasthana 4 (p. 35) lists Vidanga sixth among ten Krimighna and singles out nobody. The 'foremost' statement is a different chapter and 244 pages later, Sutrasthana 25 at p. 279.

THE TEMPERATURE IS CARRIED BY A MODERN TRANSLATION, NOT THE ORIGINAL. 'Hot in potency' is K. R. Srikantha Murthy's 2001 English rendering. The excerpt is verbatim with respect to Murthy, not with respect to Bhavamishra's Sanskrit, which I did not read. Anyone treating this as a 16th-century primary quotation should know a 21st-century translator stands between them and the text.

EDITORIAL INSERTION NOT IN THE SOURCE. The claimed excerpt adds '[and]' before 'enlargement of the [abdomen]'. The text runs 'cures colic, flatulence, enlargement of the abdomen, mitigates kapha and vata' with no conjunction. Bracketed, so honest, but it is an addition rather than a restoration.

INCONSISTENT HANDLING OF OCR DEFECTS. In the Thomson citation (H108) the finder bracketed OCR corruptions; here two Charaka OCR errors ('amthelmintics', 'Limbelia') were silently normalised. Same practice should apply to both.
Astringent and bitter rasa in the row's taste field have no support in the cited Bhavaprakasa entry.
The citation names the Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India as standardising authority; that work is forbidden as energetics support and must not be leaned on for these rasa/virya values.
As stored: no url, no verse number, no translator, year given only as 'classical'. Unresolvable without the reconstruction the finder did by hand.

results.whatIFound: I downloaded https://www.henriettes-herb.com/eclectic/kings/ferula-asaf.html myself (HTTP 200, 23,739 bytes). Both quoted passages match character for character. From Description, quoting the U.S.P.: 'It has a persistent, alliaceous odor, and a bitter, alliaceous, acrid taste.' From Action, Medical Uses, and Dosage: 'Its properties are stimulant, antispasmodic, expectorant, emmenagogue, and vermifuge (Ed.). Improper in inflammatory conditions of the system, but of marked value in purely functional nervous disorders, with excitability, and as a gastric stimulant in gastro-intestinal atony, with flatulence.' The History section does describe the preparation as claimed: 'plants under four years are not made use of', 'the soil is removed from its crown. About 40 days afterward a thin slice is cut off transversely from its top', repeated 'until no more juice can be obtained'. Separately I checked the finder's counter-claim myself: I downloaded 本草綱目 (四庫全書本)/卷34 (122,482 bytes) and the 阿魏 entry (木之一, 香木類, tagged 唐本草, moved from 草部) reads 氣味辛平無毒 — pungent, NEUTRAL, non-toxic. Confirmed, one occurrence in the file, and it belongs to 阿魏 (the adjacent 樟腦 reads 辛熱, 蘆薈 reads 苦寒, so the parse is unambiguous).
results.supportsTheClaim: Supports TASTE verbatim (bitter, alliaceous, acrid). Supports the indications: antispasmodic, expectorant, gastric stimulant in gastro-intestinal atony with flatulence, croup, pertussis, hysteria, flatulent colic, chronic catarrh, and 'dry, deep-seated and stubborn' bronchial cough. Supports part used (gum-resin from the root) and the preparation method. DOES NOT support any temperature. King's assigns none, and the one classical Chinese authority the citation itself invokes for the TCM lens assigns 平 (neutral), which contradicts 'Warm, trending hot' rather than supporting it.
concerns: The row's temperature 'Warm, trending hot' has no support in the cited primary text and is actively contradicted by the citation's own named Chinese authority: Bencao Gangmu gives 阿魏 as 辛平 (pungent, neutral). I verified this from my own download of 卷34, not from the finder's report.

The Bencao Gangmu A Wei indications are heavily demonological — 除邪鬼蟲毒, 治風邪鬼疰, and an 附方 headed 辟鬼除邪. Under the worldview filter that material cannot be surfaced as supporting evidence, which leaves the Chinese entry contributing little beyond 消肉積 and the anthelmintic sense.

The citation string bundles Ellingwood's American Materia Medica, which is on the forbidden list for energetics support, and 'Potter's Compendium' with no edition or year, so its pre/post-1900 status cannot be settled.
Small overstatement in the support claim: King's says 'plants under four years are not made use of', i.e. four years and over. The claim renders this as 'plants over four years old'.

King's never uses the word 'carminative'. The nearest support is 'gastric stimulant in gastro-intestinal atony, with flatulence' and 'flatulent colic'. Close, but the word should not be presented as quoted.

results.herb: Capillaris Wormwood (Yin Chen, Yin Chen Hao) — Artemisia capillaris
results.whatIFound: From my own download of the Sun Xingyan recension, the string 味苦，平。主風濕寒熱邪氣，熱結、黃膽。 occurs exactly once, character for character. The entry heading is 茵陳 (with a parenthetical 《御覽》作茵蒿), and the 上經 index lists 茵陳 in the 草上品 run between 景天 and 杜若, matching the entry's actual position between those two entries in the body text. I confirmed both secondary readings myself: the Wu Pu gloss reads 《吳普》曰：因塵，神農、岐伯、雷公：苦，無毒；黃帝：辛，無毒, and the 案 note ends 據此，知舊作茵陳蒿，非. The full entry continues past the quoted portion with 久服，輕身、益氣、耐老。生邱陵阪岸上。
results.supportsTheClaim: Supports taste Bitter (苦), the wind-damp indication (風濕), the heat-binding indication (熱結), and decisively the jaundice claim that is this row's whole clinical identity — 黃膽 is named outright. It does NOT support the stored temperature: the classic says 平, neutral. It does NOT support 'Pungent' in the main text; that reading exists only in the appended Wu Pu gloss and only on Huangdi's authority against three others. It does NOT support attributing the name 'Yin Chen Hao' to this text.
concerns: TEMPERATURE CONTRADICTION, the Ginkgo failure shape, independently confirmed. The row records 'Cool (slightly cold)'. The cited classic states 味苦，平 — bitter, NEUTRAL. 平 is not a hedge or an absence; it is the classic's explicit third option and this entry chose it, in a recension where neighbouring entries freely use 微寒 (蔓荊實), 寒, 溫 and 微溫. The source affirmatively says something other than what the row claims.

'Pungent' is rescuable only as a minority attribution inside the Wu Pu gloss (黃帝：辛), against 苦 from Shennong, Qibo and Leigong in the same line. If it is published it must be labelled as such, not presented as the classic's reading.

NAME PROBLEM THE CITATION GETS BACKWARDS, confirmed. Sun Xingyan heads the entry 茵陳 and his case-note argues the longer form is wrong: 據此，知舊作茵陳蒿，非. The citation calls the herb 'Yin Chen Hao' and attributes that name to the one text that rejects it.
ORTHOGRAPHY. The recension reads 黃膽; modern standard for jaundice is 黃疸. Quoted as it stands. Anyone grepping this file for 黃疸 gets a false negative, which may be why this row went unchecked.

The excerpt stops mid-entry at 黃膽。 without an ellipsis, dropping 久服，輕身、益氣、耐老。生邱陵阪岸上。 The cut falls on a sentence boundary so nothing is distorted, but the quotation is partial and is not marked as such.

results.whatIFound: Downloaded https://www.henriettes-herb.com/eclectic/kings/commiphora.html (HTTP 200, 29,543 bytes) and stripped to text. Page title and article heading are both "Myrrha (U. S. P.)—Myrrh." Every one of the eight quoted fragments is present character-for-character: (Description) "translucent on the edges, sometimes marked with whitish veins; odor balsamic; taste aromatic, bitter and acrid"; (Action) "Myrrh is stimulant, especially to mucous tissues. It also exerts an antiseptic influence, and is used to promote expectoration, as well as menstruation."; "Large doses accelerate the pulse, augment the heat of the body, cause gastric heat and burning, great sweating and marked prostration"; "It is generally used in enfeebled conditions of the body, and has been found useful in cases of excessive mucous secretion"; "Its property of restraining the mucous discharges is observed to be most pronounced upon the renal and bronchial tract."; "It is contraindicated by arterial excitement or fever."; "Myrrh was formerly used as a dressing for indolent ulcers to promote granulation and alter the character of the discharges."; "Topically, it is a very useful application to indolent sores, gangrenous ulcers, and aphthous or sloughy sore throat, spongy or ulcerated conditions of the gums, caries of the teeth, etc." Official drug line confirms species and part: "A gum-resin obtained from Commiphora Myrrha (Nees), Engler"—(U. S. P.). I independently confirmed /eclectic/kings/myrrha.html returns HTTP 404, as the finder said.
results.supportsTheClaim: Supports TASTE bitter and acrid (= pungent) directly via the U.S.P. description. Supports stimulant, antiseptic, expectorant, emmenagogue, and the ulcerated/boggy-tissue and lax-pallid-membrane indications, all verbatim. Does NOT support ASTRINGENT in any capacity — see concerns. Supports TEMPERATURE = Warm only INFERENTIALLY, and the finder overstates this. "Large doses accelerate the pulse, augment the heat of the body, cause gastric heat and burning" is a description of an OVERDOSE effect, not an assignment of a thermal grade to the drug; King's nowhere calls myrrh warm, warming, heating or stimulantly hot. "It is contraindicated by arterial excitement or fever" is corroborative but again is an indication rule, not a temperature. The finder's phrase "supports temperature = Warm directly and unusually explicitly" should be downgraded to "strongly consistent with Warm, but the source assigns no temperature."
concerns: THE FINDER'S OWN CONCERN NOTE IS WRONG AND UNDERSTATES THE PROBLEM. The note says "'Astringent' is listed as a taste on the row but King's gives it only as an action." King's does not give it at all. I grepped the stripped text and the raw HTML for astringen[a-z]* — ZERO occurrences in the entire Myrrha entry. If the row carries Astringent as a taste, this citation supports it neither as taste nor as action, and the finder's softened framing would let it through.

Quotation-boundary splice. In the source, the closing quotation mark and the "—(U. S. P.)" attribution fall after "...should be rejected", not after "acrid". The excerpt relocates them so the U.S.P. quotation appears to end at "acrid". All words are genuine and still U.S.P., but the punctuation as presented is not what the page shows.

Section-name locator is inexact. The page has two separate headings, "History." and "Description." There is no "History and Description" section on this page (unlike the Quassia page, which genuinely has one). The U.S.P. description quote is under "Description." alone.
The stored url being the King's index rather than commiphora.html is confirmed as a real navigability defect: a reader following the citation's own wording to myrrha.html gets a 404 (verified).

results.whatIFound: BHAVAPRAKASHA: downloaded https://archive.org/download/bhavaprakash/bhavprakash-2_djvu.txt (HTTP 200, 1,711,925 bytes) to my own directory. The heading अथ सारिवाद्वयस्य गुणानाह sits at character offset 401,181 and the verse begins at 401,209. Whitespace-normalized, the claimed OCR string 'सारिवायुगरं स्वादु रिनग्धं श॒क्रकरं गुड । अधिमान्द्ादचिश्वासकासामविषनाशनम्‌ । दोषनत्रयासप्रद्रञ्वरातीसारना शनम्‌ ॥' matches the file EXACTLY. The running page header a few lines later reads 'गाद्धच्यादिषगैः . ४२७.' — Guduchyadi varga, page 427, confirming both varga and page. The verse number is OCR'd as ॥ २६८ ॥ in the Sanskrit line and ॥ २३८॥ in the Hindi gloss (both garbled), but the immediately preceding verse is ॥ २१७ ॥ = 217, so 218 is the correct number. KING'S: downloaded hemidesmus.html (HTTP 200). Article heading 'Hemidesmus.—Indian Sarsaparilla.', official drug 'The root of Hemidesmus indicus, Robert Brown'. The sentence "It is brownish externally, has a feeble, bitter taste, and a peculiar aromatic odor, somewhat like that of sassafras, but which has been compared to that of new hay." is present verbatim.
results.supportsTheClaim: Bhavaprakasha supports Sweet (स्वादु) and Moist/unctuous (स्निग्ध) and the indication list. King's supports Bitter and the venereal/cutaneous/kidney/scrofula indications, and confirms species and part (root). NEITHER SUPPORTS 'Cool' — I searched the whole Bhavaprakasha region 401,100–403,000 for शीत, शीतल, उष्ण and वीर्य and got ZERO hits; the half-verse states guna (स्निग्ध, गुरु) and rasa (स्वादु) and no virya at all. King's Hemidesmus contains zero thermal vocabulary (cool/cold/warm/refrigerant = 0). I also checked the two 'sweet' hits in King's hemidesmus.html — both are in the Gymnema sylvestre RELATED SPECIES paragraph about abolishing the sense of sweetness, not a taste attribution to Hemidesmus. So King's supports only Bitter, not Sweet.
concerns: Confirmed: the verse governs सारिवाद्वय, the PAIR. The Hindi gloss under it reads 'दोनों शारिवा' (both sarivas) and the note names श्वेत (= अनन्तमूल) and कृष्ण. BCGM's 酸棗 entry, marked 本經上品, carries the head line 酸棗氣味酸平無毒 with the sub-gloss 時珍曰仁味甘氣平 — Li Shizhen assigning the KERNEL a SEPARATE reading, sweet and neutral, distinct from the fruit's sour. And in 發明: 恭曰本經用實療不得眠不用言仁今方皆用仁 (Su Gong: 'the Benjing uses the FRUIT... it does not speak of the kernel; today's formulas all use the kernel'); 宗奭曰酸棗經不言用仁而今天下皆用之 (Kou Zongshi: 'the classic does not speak of using the kernel, yet now everyone does'); 時珍曰酸棗實味酸性收故主肝病寒熱結氣酸痺久泄臍下滿痛之症其仁甘而潤故熟用療膽虚不得眠煩渴虚汗之證 (Li Shizhen splits them explicitly: the FRUIT is sour and astringing and therefore governs the Benjing indication list; the KERNEL is sweet and moistening and therefore treats gallbladder-vacuity sleeplessness, vexation-thirst and vacuity sweating).
results.supportsTheClaim: Supports 平 (neutral) and 酸 (sour), and the damp-bi and limb-ache indications. It supports NOTHING ELSE the row claims. It does not support the sweet taste, the Moist moisture, the blood-nourishing of Heart and Liver, the insomnia/sedative use, or the sweat-astringing. And the part is wrong: the cited entry's collection note is 《名醫》曰：生河東，八月采實，陰乾，四十日成 — what is gathered and shade-dried is 實, the FRUIT. The row's part_used is the dried ripe kernel. The Chinese commentarial tradition inside BCGM states in three separate voices that the Benjing passage is about the fruit and not the kernel. A passage about the fruit does not carry the kernel's energetics, and here the sources say so directly.
concerns: PART MISMATCH, and it is not a technicality — the source tradition itself asserts it. Su Gong: 本經用實…不用言仁. This is the strongest single finding in my batch.

Every element of the row's energetics_summary (nourishes Heart and Liver blood, settles a restless spirit, astringes vacuity sweat) is absent from the cited entry. The nearest thing in it is 久服，安五臟，輕身、延年, which is generic longevity boilerplate.
Sweet is unsupported by the cited work and the row builds a mechanism on it. Moist is unsupported; 濕痹 is a damp condition TREATED, which cuts the other way.

CONSTRUCTIVE, and it is exact: everything the row wants is available in Bencao Gangmu (1596) juan 36, 酸棗 entry, and only there. 時珍曰仁味甘氣平 gives sweet + neutral FOR THE KERNEL specifically; 其仁甘而潤 gives the moistening; 熟用療膽虚不得眠煩渴虚汗之證 gives the insomnia and the vacuity-sweat indication. Repointing the primary citation from Shennong to BCGM juan 36 fixes the taste, the moisture, the part, the insomnia use and the sweat-astringing in one move, and keeps the temperature at Neutral.

Textual note for whoever writes this: BCGM quotes the Benjing indication string as 四肢酸痛 where Sun Xingyan prints 四肢酸疼. The claimed excerpt matches Sun Xingyan, which is the recension it cites, so it is correct as written — but do not treat the two as interchangeable strings.
Year field 'c. 200 CE (recension 1799)' is at least honest here, unlike H139 and H294.

I grepped the entire 21 KB entry, case-insensitively, for cool, cold, bitter, astringent and dry: ZERO occurrences of any of them. That is not weak evidence of absence, it is total.

results.supportsTheClaim: Supports Sweet (甘) in the formal 氣味 position in both works. Supports the dried-fruit part via 白露後方可采摘晒焙令乾成朶 and the 校正 relocation into the fruit chapter. It DOES NOT support 'Warm', and the contradiction is three-deep: Shennong 味甘，平; BCGM head line 氣味甘平無毒; and Li Shizhen stating the point in his own voice in 發明 — 葢荔枝性熱而龍眼性和平也, lychee's nature is hot whereas longan's nature is harmonious and neutral. That last is a deliberate comparative denial of warmth.
concerns: CONFIRMED CONTRADICTION on temperature, and it is the strongest of the three Chinese temperature contradictions in this batch because Li Shizhen refutes 'warm' explicitly rather than merely printing 平.

The only warm reading anywhere is Su Gong's bracketed dissent 恭曰甘酸温 inside BCGM's own 氣味 gloss. I read it at offset 4,484. It is a sub-note overridden by the head line above it and by Li Shizhen's 發明 below it, and it also carries 酸 (sour), which the row presumably does not store. Resting 'Warm' on it means adopting half of a minority gloss and discarding the other half.

GLYPH VARIANTS in the claimed excerpt, worth recording so nobody re-greps and thinks the passage is missing: the claim writes 溫/補虛/蓋/虛煩 where the Siku wikitext has 温/補虚/葢/虚煩. Attribution: BCGM marks longan 别録中品 and credits the 主治 to 别錄, not to 本經. Sun Xingyan does print it as Benjing text, so the citation is defensible, but 'c. 200 CE' asserts as settled something the tradition itself disputes.
The finder is right that 久服強魂聰明輕身不老通神明 is not a plain 'benefits vital energy and the mind' — it is longevity and spirit-communication boilerplate and should not be paraphrased into a clinical claim.

The character offset ~62119 the finder gives is correct, which means the discrepancy was visible at the point of retrieval.

SPECIES MISMATCH inside the named primary, confirmed independently: King's official drug is Rheum officinale; the row is Rheum palmatum. The quoted taste and action passages describe the officinale root.

The citation buries the only source that carries the energetics. Shen Nong Ben Cao Jing is named third inside a primary citation whose author field reads 'King's American Dispensatory', so 'Cold' is structurally attributed to a work that never says it.
