Every line number in the locator is correct. The heading sits at char offset 18,817, inside 卷一·上經. Line 560 carries the 吳普 gloss including 扁鵲：酸，無毒 and 李氏：生溫，熟寒, both verbatim as the finder reports. Line 562 reads 《名醫》曰：一名胡　，一名香果。其葉，名蘼蕪。 and the 蘼蕪 entry's own gloss (line 574 region) reads 《名醫》曰：一名茳蘺，芎　苗也. Transcription corruption confirmed: 藭 is lost throughout, replaced by U+3000 ideographic space.
results.supportsTheClaim: Supports taste 辛 (pungent) and temperature 溫 (warm) directly, and supports the indication set closely: 中風入腦，頭痛 for the head-directed action, 婦人血閉無子 for the blood-chamber/gynaecological action, 寒痹 and 筋攣緩急 for pain and unblocking, 金創 for wound use. Does NOT support any moisture value — no moisture concept appears. This is the best-supported citation in the batch and I could not refute any part of it.
concerns: Confirmed and worth surfacing per the working agreement: the cited source contradicts itself on the two energetics the row publishes flat. Line 560 records 扁鵲：酸 (sour) against the main text's 辛, and 李氏：生溫，熟寒 (warm raw, cold cooked) against a flat 溫. The row states 'Pungent / Warm' with no indication that its own named source carries dissent.

Naming and species continuity: the classical drug is 芎藭; 'Chuan Xiong' is a post-Song regional designation and Ligusticum chuanxiong is a modern binomial. The excerpt cannot by itself establish that the classical 芎藭 is the row's latin_name.

Transcription corruption in the Wikisource copy (藭 lost to a full-width blank throughout) does not touch the quoted line, which I verified is clean, but it means any future automated re-check searching for 芎藭 will return zero hits and look like a refutation. Worth recording in the citation note.

In the row's favour and confirmed verbatim: the source imposes a freshness constraint the row does not carry — the dried root loses much of its virtue, and King's attributes therapeutic failures to old material.

results.herb: Cordyceps (Dong Chong Xia Cao, Ophiocordyceps sinensis)
results.whatIFound: Two separate findings. (1) The quoted text IS verbatim — but in Wu Yiluo's 本草從新, not in the work the citation's author and year fields name. I downloaded the zh.wikisource 本草從新 raw text myself: 177,032 characters, exactly as the finder reports. At offset 21,620 the text reads, character-for-character including the mixed simplified glyphs: 冬虫夏草 / 補肺腎。/ 甘平保肺。益腎止血。化痰已劳嗽。四川嘉定府所產者最佳。雲南贵州所出者次之。冬在土中。身活如老蚕。有毛能动。至夏則毛出土上。連身俱化爲草。若不取。至冬則復化爲虫。 It stands between 開金锁 (21,537) and 锦地罗 (21,715), exactly as claimed. The postface at 176,888 carries 乾隆丁丑 and at 176,610 凡七百二十有餘種. (2) It is NOT in the Shennong Ben Cao Jing. I searched my own 242 KB copy of the Sun Xingyan recension for 冬蟲, 夏草, 蟲草 and 冬虫: zero hits for all four. I also downloaded 本草備要 (143,404 characters, matching the finder's figure exactly) and searched 夏草, 冬蟲, 冬虫, 蟲草, 虫草: zero hits for all five.
results.supportsTheClaim: Supports sweet taste (甘), Lung and Kidney tonification (補肺腎 / 保肺 / 益腎), stopping bleeding (止血), transforming phlegm (化痰), taxation cough (已劳嗽), Sichuan provenance and the life-cycle description. It FLATLY CONTRADICTS the stored temperature: the text reads 甘平 — sweet and NEUTRAL. It does not contain 溫 anywhere in the entry, and contains no 腎陽 / yang-warming language at all.
concerns: TEMPERATURE CONTRADICTED BY THE CITED SOURCE. Row stores 'Warm' and an energetics summary built on 'warms Kidney yang'; the named text says 平. This is the withdrawn-Ginkgo failure mode repeating, and it is a contradiction, not merely an absence.

AUTHOR AND YEAR FIELDS ARE FALSE, independently verified. Cordyceps is absent from the Shennong Ben Cao Jing under every orthography I tried, in my own downloaded copy. A citation whose author and year point at a work that does not contain the herb cannot be written as filed.

THE 'EARLIER MENTION' IN WANG ANG IS UNSUPPORTED. My own 本草備要 download returns zero hits for every spelling. I cannot call it definitively false from one unproofread transcription, but nothing in the record supports it and it should be struck rather than softened.

TRANSCRIPTION QUALITY. The wikisource page carries the {{未校訂}} (not proofread) banner — I confirmed it at the end of the file — and cites ctext.org and zysj.com.cn as sources. It mixes simplified forms (冬虫夏草, 老蚕, 能动, 贵州, 劳嗽) into an otherwise traditional text. Quoting it verbatim reproduces those simplified glyphs, which will not match a traditional print edition character-for-character.

NO JUAN IS RECOVERABLE, and the finder was right to refuse to invent one. I tested this: the header links 卷一 through 卷十八 as subpages, but I fetched 本草從新/卷一 through /卷四 and every one returns HTTP 404. The subpage links are redlinks; the juan divisions genuinely do not exist in this transcription.

results.whatIFound: Same split as H249. (1) The quoted text IS verbatim in the Bencao Gangmu. I downloaded 本草綱目_(四庫全書本)/卷13 raw wikitext myself (49,058 characters — full text, NOT a table-of-contents-only page; I checked for the 卷NN上/下 trap and this juan has no upper/lower split). The juan opens '草之二　　山草類下三十九種'. 延胡索 appears in that juan's own table of contents at offset 687 marked {{SK notes|開寳}}, and the entry proper begins at offset 28,679 — exactly the offset claimed — standing between 白鮮 and 貝母. Every quoted string matches character-for-character once the {{SK notes|…}} markup is unwrapped: 釋名𤣥胡索 / 好古曰本名𤣥胡索避宋真宗諱改𤣥爲延也; 根氣味辛温無毒 / 珣曰苦甘杲曰甘辛温可升可降隂中陽也好古曰苦辛温純陽浮也; 主治破血婦人月經不調腹中結塊崩中淋露産後諸血病 … 活血利氣止痛通小便{{SK notes|時珍}}; 時珍曰𤣥胡索味苦㣲辛氣温 … 能行血中氣滯氣中血滯故專治一身上下諸痛用之中的妙不可言. The 集解 opens 藏器曰延胡索生奚國從安東來根如半夏色黄, confirming the Chen Cangqi attribution. (2) It is NOT in the Shennong Ben Cao Jing, which is what the citation's author and year fields name: I searched my own copy of the Sun Xingyan recension for 延胡, 玄胡 and 𤣥胡 — zero hits for all three.
results.supportsTheClaim: Against the Bencao Gangmu the support is genuine and strong: temperature Warm from the head 氣味 line 辛温無毒 and from 好古曰苦辛温; taste Bitter + Pungent from 好古曰苦辛温; and Li Shizhen's mechanism sentence (能行血中氣滯，氣中血滯，故專治一身上下諸痛) underwrites the row's blood-and-qi stagnation pain summary independently, in words the database does not store. Against the source the citation actually names by author and year (Shennong, c. 200 CE) it supports nothing, because the herb is absent from that work.
concerns: METADATA POINTS AT A WORK THAT DOES NOT CONTAIN THIS HERB. Author 'Shennong Ben Cao Jing' and year 'c. 200 CE' against a title text saying Li Shizhen 1596. Verified absent from Shennong under three orthographies. As filed, the citation is unwritable; the fix is metadata-only.

DATING INSIDE THE CITATION IS WRONG IN THE OTHER DIRECTION TOO. The Bencao Gangmu itself marks the entry 宋開寳 — the Kaibao Bencao, c. 973 CE — and the juan's own table of contents repeats 開寳. A citation title asserting a Tang-era c. 720 first record is only partly supportable: 藏器曰 (Chen Cangqi) is quoted in 集解, but BCGM's own source-attribution for the entry is Song.

THE ROW SILENTLY PICKS ONE WITNESS ON TASTE. The same head line records three disagreeing readings — 珣曰苦甘 (bitter, sweet), 杲曰甘辛温 (sweet, acrid, warm), 好古曰苦辛温 (bitter, acrid, warm). The row matches Wang Haogu. Legitimate, but it must be attributed rather than presented as the reading.

SUSPICION CHECK: 好古曰苦辛温 does hand the row its exact stored taste pair and temperature in one clause, which is the pattern that should raise suspicion. I checked for fabrication and did not find it — the entry is at the claimed offset, between the claimed neighbours, in a juan whose contents list I independently confirmed, and the excerpt carries several clauses (可升可降隂中陽也, 純陽浮也, the two case histories) that the database does not store and could not have generated.
The excerpt truncates 入手足太隂經 off the end of the 氣味 gloss without an ellipsis, while marking its other two elisions with ……. Minor, but it should be made consistent before writing.

results.whatIFound: Downloaded both entries myself. Verbatim (the locator lowercases the leading 'The'). And in its 'Action, Medical Uses, and Dosage.': 'Small spikenard possesses alterative properties, and is used in decoction or syrup as a substitute for sarsaparilla in all cases where an alterative is required. It is likewise used in pulmonary diseases.' Verbatim. The nudicaulis entry also states the DRIED rhizome has 'a mawkish, somewhat oily, unpleasant taste' — verbatim, as the finder warned.
results.supportsTheClaim: Supports the Pungent/aromatic taste and the balsamic-aromatic language directly, and supports the atonic-cough and catarrh indications almost as the row's entire therapeutic claim. Does NOT support Sweet for this species — the word 'sweet' occurs zero times in the racemosa entry; 'saccharine' occurs only in the A. nudicaulis entry, a different species, and only of the FRESH root. Does NOT support Bitter — 'bitter' occurs zero times in either entry. Does NOT support Warm or any moisture value — 'warm' and 'cold' occur zero times in either entry. Does NOT support any diaphoretic action — 'diaphoretic' occurs zero times in either entry.
concerns: CROSS-SPECIES BORROWING FOR A STORED TASTE. Sweet rests entirely on 'saccharine' in the A. nudicaulis entry. This is the congener problem the project has already been burned by, running in the opposite direction from the withdrawn Spikenard citation: the row is correctly A. racemosa, but one of its three tastes is imported from A. nudicaulis. Worse, the borrowed word applies to the FRESH root, and the same entry calls the DRIED root 'mawkish, somewhat oily, unpleasant'.
BITTER IS UNSOURCED IN EITHER ENTRY. I counted: zero occurrences of 'bitter' across both. The row stores three tastes and King's supports one of them for the right species.

TEMPERATURE AND MOISTURE ARE UNSOURCED. Zero occurrences of warm/cold/moist/dry in either entry. Ellingwood (1919), the other work named in the citation title, is forbidden for energetics, so nothing in the citation can carry these fields.

'MOVES STALE CATARRH OUTWARD THROUGH THE SKIN' IS AN INFERENCE, NOT A SOURCED CLAIM. Neither entry states a diaphoretic action; the word does not appear. The only external use given is for A. nudicaulis, as a wash in shingles and indolent ulcers, which is the opposite direction of movement.

CITATION-OBJECT HYGIENE: primary and secondary both point at the King's URL, so there is no independent corroboration in this citation, while the secondary's title text lists Cook (1869), AHPA, WebMD/RxList and United Plant Savers — none of which is the work its author field or URL names.

Confirmed that BOTH permitted classics head this drug 苦平. In BCGM the 大寒 is explicitly a 别錄 attribution inside the 氣味 note, not the 綱目's own head value. If the row keeps 'Cold', the citation must be re-pointed at the 名醫別錄 (or at BCGM's quoted layer, labelled as such), not left on the Shennong.

Three incompatible classical temperatures for one herb — 平 (Shennong), 大寒 (别錄, via BCGM), 小溫 (李氏, in the Wu Pu commentary appended to the very same Shennong entry, verified at line 1690). The row cites the one work that gives none of them as 'Cold'. Per the working agreement, this is a case to surface rather than resolve.

The excerpt carries a genuine lacuna (U+3000 for 澼). Anyone re-typing it should be told it is a source defect, not a transcription error, or the next reader will 'fix' it and break the provenance chain.

results.supportsTheClaim: Supports the INDICATIONS strongly and precisely: 主風 (governs wind), 頭眩腫痛, 目欲脫, 淚出, 皮膚死肌, 惡風濕痹. concerns: TEMPERATURE CONTRADICTION confirmed at both permitted classics' head lines. Row = Cool; Shennong = 平; BCGM 卷15 head = 苦平無毒. Exactly the withdrawn-Ginkgo shape.

CORRECTION TO THE FINDER'S FRAMING, in the row's partial favour: the extra tastes and the cool reading are not simply nowhere. BCGM's 氣味 note carries '别録曰甘' (Bielu: sweet) and '杲曰苦甘寒' (Li Gao: bitter-sweet, COLD), and 時珍 writes 味兼甘苦性禀平和. So sweet, and a cold/cool reading, do exist in the classical stratum — but as later attributions inside BCGM's commentary layer, NOT in the Shennong Bencao Jing the row cites. If those values are kept they must be re-cited to that layer and labelled by attribution.

The stored citation reportedly has url: null and a locator that merely restates the title. As filed, the row was not re-findable by anyone. That is the condition under which the eleven withdrawn citations survived.

No recension is named in the stored citation. A Shennong Bencao Jing citation that does not name a reconstruction is unverifiable in principle. Add 'Sun Xingyan, 1799' and note that this recension heads the entry 鞠華 — a searcher looking for 菊花 will find nothing and may wrongly conclude the entry is absent.

results.whatIFound: Heading '==術==' is at line 266 of my copy of the Sun Xingyan raw wikitext; line 268 reads: 味苦，溫。主風寒濕痹、死肌、痙、疸。止汗，除熱，消食，作煎餌。久服，輕身、延年、不飢。一名山薊（《藝文類聚》引作山筋），生山谷。 The excerpt matches character for character up to 作煎餌。 The finder's line numbers are exact — text at 268, and the philological 案 note at line 274, which reads: 案：《說文》云：術，山薊也；《廣雅》云：山薑，朮也。白朮，牡丹也。《中山經》云：首山草多術。… The Guangya quotation the finder cites is verbatim and is genuinely there. Upper-grade placement confirmed structurally ('= 卷一·上經 =' at line 32, '= 卷二·中經 =' at line 1384; 術 at 266 falls inside 卷一). The upper-grade roster at line 36 lists '…甘草　干地黃　術　菟絲子…' — one undifferentiated 術, no 白朮/蒼朮 split anywhere in the text.
results.supportsTheClaim: Supports TEMPERATURE 溫 (warm) exactly, the bitter half of the taste (苦), damp-impediment via 風寒濕痹, digestion via 消食, and — a strong, specific match — the spontaneous-sweating claim via 止汗. It does NOT support the SWEET taste, which is simply absent from the entry and which the row uses to carry its entire Spleen-tonifying mechanism. Most importantly, it does not resolve to Atractylodes macrocephala: the source has one undifferentiated 術 that is the common ancestor of both Bai Zhu and Cang Zhu, so it cannot underwrite species-specific energetics for A. macrocephala.
concerns: SPECIES RESOLUTION IS THE REAL PROBLEM, and I confirm it. The cited text carries ONE 術. The A. macrocephala / A. lancea split postdates this source by centuries and appears nowhere in it. Attributing a monograph on A. macrocephala specifically to this entry claims a precision the source cannot deliver. If the pipeline flags species failures by verdict rather than by note, this row is the candidate — the excerpt is real, but the citation-to-species link is not.

The source's own apparatus points the name the other way, and I verified the quotation at line 274: 《廣雅》云：山薑，朮也。白朮，牡丹也 — in that early lexicon 白朮 denoted 牡丹, moutan, an unrelated plant. A citation title reading 'Zhu / Bai Zhu (Atractylodes)' therefore imports a later identification into a text that uses the name differently.

HEIGHTENED-SUSPICION CHECK APPLIED: the excerpt's 溫 matches the row's stored temperature 'Warm' exactly. I therefore re-read line 268 specifically to confirm the character is present and it is (味苦，溫). adjudication:
Everything below is read off the verification record you supplied. I did not re-open any source myself, so every claim here is "the verifiers reported X," not "I confirmed X." Where the record contradicts itself, I say so rather than picking.

---

## 1. How many survived, and what that rate actually means

124 of the 126 recovered excerpts got a verdict. Two recovered excerpts have no verdict in the record at all. Nobody has explained where they went, and until someone does, treat them as unverified, not as passes.

Of the 124 judged: 112 verbatim-confirmed, 12 failed. That is a 90.3% verbatim pass rate.

That number is flattering and you should not take comfort in it. Compare the two conditions honestly:

| | Unchecked (the 201) | This pass (the 126) |
|---|---|---|
| Bad citations found | 15, after they reached production and had to be withdrawn | 12, caught before load |
| When found | Two rounds of post-publication cleanup | Pre-load |
| What "found" caught | Fabrication and unsupportability | Verbatim accuracy only |

The recovery-plus-verification process is working. It catches roughly the same volume of garbage the withdrawals did, but catches it early. That is the good news and it is real.

Here is the bad news, and it is bigger. The 90% figure measures one thing only: is the quoted string physically present in the named book. It does not measure whether the quote supports the herb row it is attached to. On that second question the pass rate collapses to roughly 28%. Details in section 4.

One housekeeping problem with the record itself, which matters because you are going to be asked to trust these counts. Part A is labeled "FAILED EXCERPTS (11)" and lists 12. The 12 entries reconcile exactly against the type breakdown (2 locator, 7 species/part, 3 not-in-source), so the header is simply a miscount. Slice 2 claims 62 confirmed rows and lists 55. Part B claims 48 and lists 50. Net, 105 of the 112 confirmed rows are visible; 7 are not. Do not let anyone reconcile these by rounding.

---

## 2. The rejects, named

**The three classified NOT_IN_SOURCE. These are fabrications that got through the recovery pass.**

**H136 Fo-Ti (He Shou Wu).** The citation names the Shennong Ben Cao Jing, c. 200 CE. The verifier downloaded the Sun Xingyan recension, 242,119 bytes, and searched it. 何首烏 returns zero hits. Even bare 首烏 returns zero. He Shou Wu is not in that book. It cannot be, it is a Tang-era entrant. The citation names a work that does not contain the plant.

**H249 Cordyceps.** The quoted text is real, but it is in Wu Yiluo's Bencao Congxin, not in the work the author and year fields name. The excerpt was verified at offset 21,620 of a self-downloaded copy of the wrong book. Right words, wrong spine.

**H271 Corydalis (Yan Hu Suo).** Same shape. The text is verbatim in the Bencao Gangmu, juan 13, and the verifier confirmed the juan is full text and not a table of contents. It is not in the work the citation's author and year fields name.

That pattern, the text being genuine but living in a different book from the one the citation credits, is the same disguised-source failure that produced withdrawals before. It is not a typo. A reader who checks the named book finds nothing and concludes you invented it.

**The nine other hard failures.**

Two locator failures. **H174 Wild Indigo**: the quoted King's text is 100% genuine, every fragment present once, character for character, but the locator names an entry heading, "BAPTISIA (U. S. P.)—BAPTISIA", that does not exist on the page. **H172 Pleurisy Root**: the locator names "ASCLEPIAS (U. S. P.)—PLEURISY ROOT". Checked against two independent copies including the printed 1898 book. The heading is "Asclepias (U. S. P.)—Asclepias." No such heading as claimed.

Seven species or part failures. Every one of these is a genuine quote pointed at the wrong plant or the wrong part of the right plant.

## 4. Genuine quote, wrong claim. This is the real exposure.

Of the 105 confirmed rows visible in the record, **76 carry at least one stored field that the cited source does not support or actively contradicts.** That is 72% of the rows that "passed."

This is a completely different failure from a bad quote, and it is the one verbatim checking cannot see. Split it two ways.

**Silent sources, roughly 46 rows.** The quote is perfect and the book simply does not say the thing. The dominant case by far is temperature on Eclectic sources. King's American Dispensatory describes action and dosage. It does not assign humoral temperature. It structurally cannot. So no amount of correct quotation from King's will ever underwrite a Warm or Cool field. The verifiers proved this negatively rather than by impression, running zero-occurrence sweeps for thermal vocabulary across whole monographs: H101 White Oak, H106 Juniper (zero thermal words in 19KB), H129 Cascara, H133 Saw Palmetto, H204 Grindelia, H205 Jamaica Dogwood, H211 Wahoo, H220 Stillingia, H236 Colic Root, H250 False Unicorn, H297 Balmony, H287 Bogbean, H108 Bayberry, H114 White Horehound, H115 Wormwood, H117 Rue, H143 Buchu, H216 Fringe Tree, H105 Prickly Ash, H124 Clove, H202 Cranesbill.

Watch for the traps inside this group, because they are how the field got populated in the first place. H115 Wormwood: the only "warm" in the entry is "used, however, as a warm fomentation for sprains," an instruction about a poultice. H155 Parsley: the only warmth language belongs to apiol, an isolated constituent at 7 to 15 grain doses. H156 Spearmint: "coolness in the mouth during inhalation" is a transient oral sensation, not a thermal grading. H124 Clove: "stimulant" is an Eclectic action word and treating it as a temperature is exactly the category error this review exists to catch.

Two rows deserve separate mention because they show the field inventing its own authority. **H202 Cranesbill** justifies Cool in-field with "A tannin astringent is cooling and condensing." That is the row reasoning from chemistry, sitting in a position where a citation is expected. **H204 Grindelia** appeals to "herbalist tradition," which is an unnamed authority and is not a citation.

**Outright contradictions, roughly 30 rows.** Worse than silence, because the citation lends authority to a value the named work refutes. Fifteen of these are temperature, and they are the Ginkgo failure repeating fifteen times:

H173 White Peony (row Cool, source 平 neutral), H177 Forsythia (平), H240 Asafoetida (辛平), H267 Yin Chen Hao (味苦，平), H139 Kudzu, H142 Baikal Skullcap (平, not Cold), H169 Chrysanthemum (平 at both permitted classics' head lines), H170 Goji (味苦，寒 against a stored Sweet/Neutral), H183 Pinellia (平, not Warm), H246 Longan (Li Shizhen refutes warm explicitly), H270 Cornelian Cherry, H272 Eucommia (辛平), H282 Moutan (寒 vs stored Cool), H206 Manjistha ("hot in potency" right there on p.190, against a stored Cool), H299 Cape Aloes.

H173 White Peony is the one I would pull first. The row stores Cool and Sour. Shennong says 苦，平, bitter and neutral, and Bencao Gangmu juan 14 independently confirms Shennong's reading. Sour exists in that recension only as Lei Gong's minority reading inside a list of five disagreeing authorities. Cool and Sour are available pre-1900, from 别錄 and 元素 via BCGM juan 14, but from a different work than the one cited. This row must not ship with the Shennong citation attached to its temperature or taste.

The taste contradictions are the same disease: H149 Caraway (King's says "sweetish, spicy"; bitter has zero occurrences in the whole entry), H259 Poke ("taste sweetish and acrid", the source pairs acrid with sweetish, not bitter), H293 Rhatany (bitter: zero occurrences), H109 Myrrh (astringen\* returns zero across the entire entry, so the finder's own note understated it), H118 Pumpkin Seed ("taste bland and oily" against a stored Sweet), H221 Stone Root (the row's defining Astringent against a source that says spicy and pungent), H252 Hydrangea (the page affirmatively reports no tannin), H166 Black Haw (bark is "very bitter, slightly aromatic"; the sweetness belongs to the berry only), H205 Jamaica Dogwood ("sweet" does not occur once).

And one plain factual error, confirmed at three places: **H234 Summer Savory**. The row says hot and dry in the second degree. Culpeper's catalogue says third, and both his third-degree tables list it.

Separately from field support, there is a smaller cluster of quote-integrity problems that would fail a character-for-character diff even though nothing was invented: unmarked elisions at H134 Bupleurum (a splice with no ellipsis, and the excerpt field itself is the problem even though the finder disclosed the cut elsewhere), H176 Coptis, H183, H268, H269 Chinese Yam (this one drops a variant reading that gives BITTER for the same authorities, so it is material), H275, H280, H276. Order inversions at H122 Hyssop and H127 Senna, where bracketed ellipses imply forward continuation that the source does not have. Misquotations at H237 Broom ("almost" inserted, zero occurrences in the source) and H299 ("odour" for "odor" inside quotation marks). Non-existent section headings at H113, H225, H245. A 30-line uniform offset at H233. Off-by-one at H171.

## 5. What is safe to load

**Zero rows.** Not one row in this batch arrived unflagged. Every single entry in both slices is labeled "CONFIRMED but flagged" or failed outright. There is no clean pile.

What is safe is narrower than a row, and you should hold that distinction hard:

**112 excerpt strings are safe to store as excerpt text** (105 of them visible in this record, 7 not shown, and I would not load the 7 until someone produces them). Safe means the string is physically present in some named pre-1900 work at a locator someone can re-check. That is the entire claim. Even here, at least 10 need a transcription note or a repaired ellipsis before they can be called verbatim, and 2 were silently normalized from OCR noise (H001, H256).

**Nothing is safe to load as a citation-plus-field pair without per-field surgery.** 76 of 105 visible rows carry a field the cited source does not underwrite. Loading those attaches the authority of a real 1898 or 1596 book to a value that book refutes or never states, which is worse than an empty field, because it looks checked.

**Do not load at all, 21 rows:**

The 12 hard failures: H136, H249, H271, H174, H172, H264, H185, H168, H276, H292, H157, H163.

The 6 misclassified fabrications: H238, H138, H208, H178, H244, H188.

Three more I would hold on structural grounds: H104 (values match a work other than the one cited), H256 and H146 (author, title and URL name different books, and the forbidden source is listed primary in both).

**The closest thing to a clean row in the whole batch is H209 Pipsissewa.** The verifier tried to break it and could not: quotation accurate, entry heading exact, species explicitly the row's species, constituents check out. Even that one has a small attribution imprecision, the row saying King's "describes the fresh leaf" where the source does not scope it that way. H216 Fringe Tree is the cleanest on source, year, author, species, part and working URL, and all four of its energetics values are supported by nothing.

If a row's best case is "we could not break it, apart from this one thing," the batch is not ready.

**Before anything moves, three things need deciding by you, not by me.** First, whether Eclectic sources are permanently barred from carrying temperature and moisture, which would immediately vacate roughly 25 fields and is the single highest-leverage rule available. Second, what happens to the 15 temperature contradictions: correct the field, or swap in the source that actually says it, since admissible pre-1900 warrants exist and were identified for at least H146 (Culpeper, Gutenberg 49513 line 16230, hot and dry in the second degree) and H173 (别錄 via BCGM juan 14). Third, where the 2 verdict-less excerpts and the 7 missing confirmed rows went.

I am not recommending any write to the live database off this record.
